Washington reports first US bird flu death of 2026; health officials say risk to the public is low Respiratory viruses Agriculture See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! A microscope image shows influenza A virus subtype H5N1, commonly known as bird flu. Three cases have been reported in humans in Washington state, including one death. CDC/NIAID/AP A person in Yakima County, Washington, who caught bird flu after being exposed to infected dairy cows has died following a severe illness, county health officials said Sunday. This is the first known person in the US to die from complications from avian influenza in 2026 and the third in the US to die from bird flu since February 2024, when the virus jumped into dairy cattle for the first time. On October 31, the Yakima County Health District reported that a person who had come into contact with infected cattle was hospitalized with a severe case of bird flu. The person had underlying health conditions, but the county did not specify what they were. On November 1, the county reported that the person had died. Yakima County health officials said they are closely monitoring the contacts of the person who died to ensure that they didn’t pass the infection to anyone else. Ad Feedback The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recorded bird flu cases in more than 70 people in the US since 2024. Most of the people who’ve become ill have worked on farms with infected cattle or poultry. Health officials say that most cases have been mild and all have been so-called dead-end infections, in which a virus jumps from an animal to a person but doesn’t spread farther. No human-to-human transmission of bird flu has been documented in the US. Health officials say the risk to the public remains low. Related article General view of Heard Island And Mcdonald Islands. Courtesy Australian Antarctic Division/Doug Thost Thousands of baby seals died on two remote sub-Antarctic islands. Scientists now think they know why 2 min read Three cases have been identified in people in the Yakima County Health District this year: a mild case identified last month, the person who died and a third case reported over the weekend. All three Washington cases have occurred since mid-October and resulted from exposure to infected cows. The third case, like the first case, has mild symptoms and has not been hospitalized, county health district officials said. State health officials said they have reported all three cases to the CDC. So far, the agency has not included them on its bird flu dashboard. Tracking bird flu cases in humans Since October 8, 33 dairy herds infected with the H5N1 bird flu virus have been reported in Washington. The state is urging people who work at the dairies to wear personal protective equipment and report their symptoms if they feel ill. Dr. Dave Atteberry, the public health officer for the Yakima health district, said the dairies with infected cows were found in early October through milk testing by the Washington State Department of Agriculture and the US Department of Agriculture. Public health workers with the county then reached out to the affected farms and enrolled dairy workers in a text-based health screening tool that checks daily for symptoms including cough, fever or red eyes. If the workers report any, the health department follows up with additional questions, Atteberry told CNN last month. “We’re throwing a large net so that we capture everybody that that potentially could be getting exposed, and then we’re able to focus our attention on those individuals that are exposed, and then we get them treated,” Atteberry said last month. On October 15, a dairy worker in the county tested positive for mild H5N1. It was the first human case reported in nearly a year. Related article Aster, a mink rescued from a fur farm, runs around the home of Linda Maretich, where Rocky Mountain Mink Refuge is based, in Saratoga Springs, Utah, on Sept. 26, 2026. Aster was brought to the refuge in 2024 with neck and abdominal injuries. Julie Leopo for ProPublica Bird flu is raging on a mink farm. It could spark a human pandemic, experts say, but officials won’t act. 16 min read Not all states are approaching bird flu the same way. ProPublica recently reported that Utah’s Department of Agriculture and Food agreed to share information about bird flu outbreaks on farms as long as health officials didn’t take steps to track workers’ health. This patchwork state-by-state approach to monitoring bird flu infections in people is concerning, said Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, who directs the Pandemic Center at Brown University’s School of Public Health. “I just think that our our picture of H5N1 is the murkiest it’s ever been,” Nuzzo said. Nuzzo said this bird flu uptick at dairies in Washington, which has coincided with the very early circulation of seasonal influenza on the Pacific Coast, sets the table for the H5N1 virus to swap pieces of its genome with seasonal flu viruses. A big change like that could potentially give the virus the tools it needs to better infect humans. “That is the bad scenario. So when you have an uptick in bird flu activity corresponding with human flu season, that just increases my worry even more that we could have a mix that we don’t want to have,” she said. Atteberry said farm workers who test positive are given antiviral medication with the goal of treating their symptoms as well as lowering their viral load to reduce the chance they could pass it to others. “Even though we haven’t seen that biologically be possible yet,” Atteberry said. “We’re doing it out of an abundance of caution.” Respiratory viruses Agriculture See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Washington reports first US bird flu death of 2026; health officials say risk to the public is low Respiratory viruses Agriculture See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! A microscope image shows influenza A virus subtype H5N1, commonly known as bird flu. Three cases have been reported in humans in Washington state, including one death. CDC/NIAID/AP A person in Yakima County, Washington, who caught bird flu after being exposed to infected dairy cows has died following a severe illness, county health officials said Sunday. This is the first known person in the US to die from complications from avian influenza in 2026 and the third in the US to die from bird flu since February 2024, when the virus jumped into dairy cattle for the first time. On October 31, the Yakima County Health District reported that a person who had come into contact with infected cattle was hospitalized with a severe case of bird flu. The person had underlying health conditions, but the county did not specify what they were. On November 1, the county reported that the person had died. Yakima County health officials said they are closely monitoring the contacts of the person who died to ensure that they didn’t pass the infection to anyone else. Ad Feedback The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recorded bird flu cases in more than 70 people in the US since 2024. Most of the people who’ve become ill have worked on farms with infected cattle or poultry. Health officials say that most cases have been mild and all have been so-called dead-end infections, in which a virus jumps from an animal to a person but doesn’t spread farther. No human-to-human transmission of bird flu has been documented in the US. Health officials say the risk to the public remains low. Related article General view of Heard Island And Mcdonald Islands. Courtesy Australian Antarctic Division/Doug Thost Thousands of baby seals died on two remote sub-Antarctic islands. Scientists now think they know why 2 min read Three cases have been identified in people in the Yakima County Health District this year: a mild case identified last month, the person who died and a third case reported over the weekend. All three Washington cases have occurred since mid-October and resulted from exposure to infected cows. The third case, like the first case, has mild symptoms and has not been hospitalized, county health district officials said. State health officials said they have reported all three cases to the CDC. So far, the agency has not included them on its bird flu dashboard. Tracking bird flu cases in humans Since October 8, 33 dairy herds infected with the H5N1 bird flu virus have been reported in Washington. The state is urging people who work at the dairies to wear personal protective equipment and report their symptoms if they feel ill. Dr. Dave Atteberry, the public health officer for the Yakima health district, said the dairies with infected cows were found in early October through milk testing by the Washington State Department of Agriculture and the US Department of Agriculture. Public health workers with the county then reached out to the affected farms and enrolled dairy workers in a text-based health screening tool that checks daily for symptoms including cough, fever or red eyes. If the workers report any, the health department follows up with additional questions, Atteberry told CNN last month. “We’re throwing a large net so that we capture everybody that that potentially could be getting exposed, and then we’re able to focus our attention on those individuals that are exposed, and then we get them treated,” Atteberry said last month. On October 15, a dairy worker in the county tested positive for mild H5N1. It was the first human case reported in nearly a year. Related article Aster, a mink rescued from a fur farm, runs around the home of Linda Maretich, where Rocky Mountain Mink Refuge is based, in Saratoga Springs, Utah, on Sept. 26, 2026. Aster was brought to the refuge in 2024 with neck and abdominal injuries. Julie Leopo for ProPublica Bird flu is raging on a mink farm. It could spark a human pandemic, experts say, but officials won’t act. 16 min read Not all states are approaching bird flu the same way. ProPublica recently reported that Utah’s Department of Agriculture and Food agreed to share information about bird flu outbreaks on farms as long as health officials didn’t take steps to track workers’ health. This patchwork state-by-state approach to monitoring bird flu infections in people is concerning, said Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, who directs the Pandemic Center at Brown University’s School of Public Health. “I just think that our our picture of H5N1 is the murkiest it’s ever been,” Nuzzo said. Nuzzo said this bird flu uptick at dairies in Washington, which has coincided with the very early circulation of seasonal influenza on the Pacific Coast, sets the table for the H5N1 virus to swap pieces of its genome with seasonal flu viruses. A big change like that could potentially give the virus the tools it needs to better infect humans. “That is the bad scenario. So when you have an uptick in bird flu activity corresponding with human flu season, that just increases my worry even more that we could have a mix that we don’t want to have,” she said. Atteberry said farm workers who test positive are given antiviral medication with the goal of treating their symptoms as well as lowering their viral load to reduce the chance they could pass it to others. “Even though we haven’t seen that biologically be possible yet,” Atteberry said. “We’re doing it out of an abundance of caution.” Respiratory viruses Agriculture See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! news.content: Loading Skip to Main Content Search How Do I? Your Government County Services Safety & Justice Home News Flash Washington State Reports First Bird Flu Outbreak in Dairy Cows News Flash Washington State Reports First Bird Flu Outbreak in Dairy Cows The Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) and the Yakima Health District recently announced an avian influenza (H5N1) outbreak in dairy cattle across Yakima and Benton counties. These mark the first known cases of bird flu in Washington dairy herds. After detecting the virus in cattle, the Yakima Health District has confirmed 3 human cases of avian influenza among Yakima County residents, including one death in a person with underlying health conditions. The individuals became ill after contact with infected cattle. There is no known human-to-human transmission in the United States at this time. WSDA is working with affected farms to investigate and test sick livestock, while DOH and local public health agencies monitor farm workers and track the situation alongside federal partners. “This latest outbreak highlights the need to stay cautious,” said Dr. Amy Harley, Health Officer for Whatcom County Health and Community Services. “Dairy and poultry workers, backyard flock owners, hunters, and anyone who comes into contact with wildlife should take precautions to protect themselves and prevent the spread of bird flu.” So far this year, Whatcom County has no reported cases of bird flu in humans, farm animals, or backyard flocks. About Avian Influenza (H5N1) Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), often called "bird flu," is a virus common in birds worldwide that can cause serious illness in birds. HPAI can also infect other animals, including wild animals and livestock. While human cases of H5N1 are rare and typically happen through close contact with infected animals without proper protective gear, sporadic cases have been reported in the U.S. since 2022. Most U.S. cases have been mild, though a small number have required hospitalization or resulted in severe illness or death. Washington's first human case occurred in October 2024 from close contact with birds at a poultry farm. The risk of avian influenza infection to the general public in Washington State remains low. The greatest influenza risk in Washington is seasonal influenza; the seasonal flu vaccine is recommended for everyone six months and older. Prevent the Spread of Bird Flu Do not touch wild birds or wild animals. Wild birds and other animals can carry avian influenza even if they appear healthy. Avoid contact with sick or dead birds or animals. Avoid contact with bird droppings or contaminated surfaces (e.g., bird feeders). Reporting sick or dead animals in Washington depends on the type of animal: Domestic birds (chickens & ducks): Report to the WSDA Avian Health Program via their online form, or call 1-800-606-3056. Livestock (including cattle): Isolate affected animals and contact your veterinarian. Report sick livestock to WSDA at 360-902-1878, or email ahealth@agr.wa.gov. Wild birds: Report sick or dead wild birds to the Washington Department of Fish & Wildlife via their online form. Your Government County Services Safety & Justice Home News Flash Washington State Reports First Bird Flu Outbreak in Dairy Cows News Flash Washington State Reports First Bird Flu Outbreak in Dairy Cows The Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) and the Yakima Health District recently announced an avian influenza (H5N1) outbreak in dairy cattle across Yakima and Benton counties. These mark the first known cases of bird flu in Washington dairy herds. After detecting the virus in cattle, the Yakima Health District has confirmed 3 human cases of avian influenza among Yakima County residents, including one death in a person with underlying health conditions. The individuals became ill after contact with infected cattle. There is no known human-to-human transmission in the United States at this time. WSDA is working with affected farms to investigate and test sick livestock, while DOH and local public health agencies monitor farm workers and track the situation alongside federal partners. “This latest outbreak highlights the need to stay cautious,” said Dr. Amy Harley, Health Officer for Whatcom County Health and Community Services. “Dairy and poultry workers, backyard flock owners, hunters, and anyone who comes into contact with wildlife should take precautions to protect themselves and prevent the spread of bird flu.” So far this year, Whatcom County has no reported cases of bird flu in humans, farm animals, or backyard flocks. About Avian Influenza (H5N1) Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), often called "bird flu," is a virus common in birds worldwide that can cause serious illness in birds. HPAI can also infect other animals, including wild animals and livestock. While human cases of H5N1 are rare and typically happen through close contact with infected animals without proper protective gear, sporadic cases have been reported in the U.S. since 2022. Most U.S. cases have been mild, though a small number have required hospitalization or resulted in severe illness or death. Washington's first human case occurred in October 2024 from close contact with birds at a poultry farm. The risk of avian influenza infection to the general public in Washington State remains low. The greatest influenza risk in Washington is seasonal influenza; the seasonal flu vaccine is recommended for everyone six months and older. Prevent the Spread of Bird Flu Do not touch wild birds or wild animals. Wild birds and other animals can carry avian influenza even if they appear healthy. Avoid contact with sick or dead birds or animals. Avoid contact with bird droppings or contaminated surfaces (e.g., bird feeders). Reporting sick or dead animals in Washington depends on the type of animal: Domestic birds (chickens & ducks): Report to the WSDA Avian Health Program via their online form, or call 1-800-606-3056. Livestock (including cattle): Isolate affected animals and contact your veterinarian. Report sick livestock to WSDA at 360-902-1878, or email ahealth@agr.wa.gov. Wild birds: Report sick or dead wild birds to the Washington Department of Fish & Wildlife via their online form. People with recreational or job-related exposure to infected birds, cattle, or other infected animals, or their environments, should take extra precautions, including wearing recommended personal protective equipment. Do not eat or drink raw or undercooked food, such as unpasteurized (raw) milk or raw cheeses, or raw meats. Do not let your pets eat or drink raw milk or other dairy products, raw pet foods, or raw meat. Get the seasonal flu vaccine. Although it does not prevent bird flu, it reduces the risk of co-infection with human and avian influenza viruses. Although the season has started early, it's not too late to benefit from the flu vaccine. Protect Your Backyard Flock Wild birds can spread bird flu to pet birds, including chickens. Backyard flock owners are strongly encouraged to take proactive steps to protect their birds and reduce the risk of spreading the virus: Cover chicken coops and runs to prevent contact with wild birds. Wear dedicated clothing and shoes when working with birds to reduce cross-contamination risk. Wash your hands before and after working with birds. Avoid all contact with wild birds or shared water sources by covering ponds with netting or fencing off areas where domestic birds can't access them. Change food and water daily. Store all feed in airtight containers. Clean and disinfect equipment that comes into contact with birds or droppings. After visiting places with poultry, change your clothing and clean your footwear before caring for your birds. For more information on avian flu, visit the avian influenza page on the WA DOH website. The response includes ongoing investigation and monitoring, though no detailed actions are outlined in the report. This case highlights the importance of vigilance in preventing human infections from animal sources.

news.source_body_en: A Yakima County resident in Washington, United States, has died from bird flu, marking the first U.S. death of the year. The individual was exposed at a dairy facility, raising concerns about zoonotic transmission from avian influenza to humans. The event was reported by Global Biodefense on November 3, 2026. While the death is confirmed, no specific case or exposure counts are provided. The risk is not explicitly stated, but the incident underscores the potential for avian influenza to spread to humans. The response includes ongoing investigation and monitoring, though no detailed actions are outlined in the report. This case highlights the importance of vigilance in preventing human infections from animal sources.
news.content_zh: 美国华盛顿州亚基马县一名居民死于禽流感,这是美国今年首例死亡病例。该个体是在一家乳品厂暴露的,引起了人们对人畜共患 传播 从 禽流感 传染给人类的担忧。Global Biodefense 于 2026 年 11 月 3 日报道了该事件。虽然死亡已得到确认,但没有提供具体病例或暴露计数。该风险并未明确说明,但该事件强调了 禽流感 传播给人类的可能性。应对措施包括正在进行的调查和监控,但报告中没有概述详细的行动。该病例凸显了保持警惕预防动物源性人类感染的重要性。

news.content_title: Utah Mink Outbreak: Virologists Say H5N1 Slipped From Cattle While USDA Watched
news.content: Ask AIReal-time News Market Earnings CallEvent Calendar More Earnings CallEvent CalendarWatchlistPodcastMarket InfluencersMore Ask AIReal-time News WatchlistHoldingsMarketEarnings CallEvent CalendarPodcastMarket Influencers Utah Mink Outbreak: Virologists Say H5N1 Slipped From Cattle While USDA Watched 2026-11-01 05:08 (GMT+0) Add preferred source An H5N1 outbreak in Utah mink has been traced genetically to the cattle-adapted B3.13 strain now circulating in US dairy herds — not to wild birds — revealing a virus that moved undetected for roughly six weeks and a surveillance system that has since stopped looking. Analysis of the outbreak preprint on the virology podcast TWiV, by hosts Rich Condit and Alan Dove alongside Vincent Racaniello, makes the case that the largest risk isn't the mink themselves but what their infection implies: each new mammalian host is another roll of the dice toward human adaptation. The same episode contrasts this with Marburg virus, where a Cell Reports study explains why the virus is harmless in its bat reservoir but lethal in people — bats mount a narrow, restrained antiviral response while humans trigger broad inflammatory damage. The report also covers rising rabies exposure costs, why measles is unlikely to escape its vaccine, and a global survey showing trust in science fell from 80% in 2020 to 72% in 2025. For investors, the through-line is that underfunded surveillance and eroding public trust are themselves systemic risks in any pandemic-exposed portfolio. Key Elements H5N1USDAUtah mink farmB3.13 genotypeMarburg virusCell ReportsGustavo PalaciosAlvin CrespoThomas PeacockWellcome Global MonitorCDCEgyptian rousette batPLOS ONEPirbright Institute Something is moving H5N1 between American farms, and the people whose job it is to track it have stopped taking samples. In August 2026, USDA inspectors collected swabs from captive mink at a farm in Salt Lake County, Utah. The virus they found was not the bird flu that arrives each season with wild waterfowl. Genetically, all ten whole-genome sequences the team analyzed belonged to B3.13 — the cattle-adapted lineage that first appeared in Texas dairy herds in March 2024 — according to a preprint discussed by virologists Rich Condit and Alan Dove on the podcast This Week in Virology. The mink outbreak matters because of what it tells us about the virus's staying power. "The longer the virus spends in mammals, the better the chances we think that it will be able to adapt to humans and establish human-to-human spread," Dove said. Cattle and mink are two very different mammals. A virus that can jump between them is a virus testing new furniture in the house. A six-week head start, and one mutation to watch The epidemiological timeline is the story here. Genetic analysis places the most recent common ancestor of the Utah mink cluster at July 4, 2026. The samples weren't collected until August 7, and detection was confirmed ten days later. That means the virus circulated in the mink sheds for roughly six weeks before anyone looked. By September 29, the outbreak was reportedly still ongoing — and no further samples had been taken after that first batch. The sequences point to a single introduction, followed by diversification. Ten genomes, one cluster, all nested inside the 2026 B3.13 cattle group alongside strains from Idaho, Texas, and Utah dairy herds. One shared mutation, PB1 K388R, appears in every mink virus — a change rarely seen in wild birds but previously documented in Spanish mink infected in October 2022. The viruses also carry PB2 M631L, a cattle mutation known to boost replication in mammals. Finding Detail Genotype B3.13, the cattle-adapted clade first seen in Texas in March 2024 Cluster structure Single introduction, then diversification — all 10 sequences in one cluster Estimated entry into mink July 4, 2026 (most recent common ancestor) Detection August 17, 2026; samples from August 7 Shared mutation PB1 K388R in all 10 mink viruses; previously seen in Spanish mink, October 2022 Pre-existing cattle mutations PB2 M631L (increases replication in mammals); neuraminidase changes linked to earlier mink outbreaks Closest relatives Texas cattle strains sampled May 2026, with a three-month gap How the virus traveled from Texas cattle to Utah mink is unknown — and the authors are candid about it. Their candidate list: shared workers, vehicles or equipment moving between farms, or feed. Mink are carnivores, often fed poultry products that travel long distances across state lines. Farm labor is precarious and mobile. "Our inability to pinpoint the source of the Utah outbreak points to large surveillance gaps for highly pathogenic avian influenza in US livestock," the authors wrote, as read by host Vincent Racaniello. The gaps run deeper than one farm. H5N1 has been detected in dairy cattle in Kansas and Washington, but no sequences exist for those herds, so their relationship to the Utah cluster is unknown. There may be unidentified infected herds near the mink farm. Utah and Idaho are two of the largest mink-producing states, and both have continuing B3.13 circulation in cattle — a coincidence the preprint's authors treat as a risk factor. The policy problem is the real outbreak Here is where the science meets the politics, and where the hosts don't hold back. By the preprint's account, neither the state nor the USDA ordered culling or monitored exposed farm workers. The USDA told the state veterinarian there was no mechanism to authorize vaccination or to compensate the producer for mink losses. Alleged fur-industry pressure has discouraged regulation. Federal interstate testing requirements apply to lactating dairy cattle, yet the virus keeps shuttling between Idaho, Texas, and Utah. Dove pushes back on the easy explanation that a different administration would simply test more. He argues the USDA has a structural conflict baked into its mission — promoting agriculture on one side, protecting public health on the other — and that farm margins are razor thin. Any intervention carries real cost and real political resistance. Poultry culling happens because export markets demand it. There is no comparable export pressure for mink pelts: 80% of the farmed mink market is in China, which means US producers have almost no domestic demand to protect — and little industry-side incentive to fund surveillance or accept a cull. Why mink in particular? "Mink could be a vessel for reassortment between human and avian strains," Condit said. Farmed mink are one of the few settings where a human-adapted influenza virus might meet a bird-adapted one inside the same animal. The preprint's own open questions read like a to-do list nobody has picked up: will the virus spread to other mink farms (SARS-CoV-2 spread across six Utah mink farms in 2020, possibly via free-roaming cats), is it still adapting to mink, and why haven't wild birds seeded North American mink outbreaks the way gulls did in Spain and Finland? For perspective on severity, consider the baseline. Avian-origin H5N1 kills up to half the people it infects. The cattle-linked B genotype has produced mostly mild human cases; the D genotype has been more severe. "When humans get avian H5N1 from birds it has a high fatality, right up to 50%," Racaniello said. "The cases associated with the B genotype from cows have been mild." The mink viruses belong to the cattle world. That is reassuring today. The question is what six more weeks — or six more months — of unchecked mammalian circulation does to that picture. Why Marburg kills us and leaves bats alone The second paper in the episode answers a question that sounds like trivia but isn't: how does a virus that is lethal to humans live peacefully inside a bat? A study in Cell Reports, led by Gustavo Palacios with co-first authors André Philippe Pastor and Shruti Sherath, compared Egyptian rousette bat cells and human cells to find out. The design was simple: hit fibroblasts with poly(I:C), a synthetic stand-in for double-stranded viral RNA, for four hours, then sequence the RNA and compare what each species switched on. Four functional gene classes emerged — human genes sitting low at baseline, bat genes sitting low at baseline, genes the bats induced strongly, and genes the humans induced strongly. The pattern is the point. Bat cells switched on a tight set of antiviral effectors such as ZBP1 and held inflammatory signals like chemokines and IL-6 in check. Human cells lit up a broad inflammatory and cytokine program plus Toll-like receptors and RIG-I pathway components, along with genes tied to necroptosis and apoptosis. The authors describe the bat response as "robust yet restrained" and the human one as "indiscriminate inflammatory amplification" — the mechanism they suspect drives the cytokine storm that makes Marburg disease so destructive. The hosts repeatedly invoke a warning from a colleague: "if you've seen one bat, you've seen one bat." Bat immunology varies wildly across species — some have a contracted type I interferon locus with constitutive interferon alpha, others have expanded interferon omega genes, some lack interferon alpha entirely. Interferon epsilon gets its own section in the paper: rousette intestinal organoids and airway cultures show elevated constitutive epsilon and interferon-stimulated genes, and a prior study concluded epsilon production drives bat immune resilience. In rousettes, epsilon is highest in brain, ovaries, and liver, absent from most immune tissues, and unchanged after infection — largely mirroring human biology. Condit raises the main methodological caveat, and it's worth hearing because it's how real science gets read. These are dermal fibroblasts — not immune cells, not endothelial cells, and not the epithelial frontline where infection starts. He checked the cell bank records and found the cells are around passage 14, subcultured enough to be effectively pure fibroblasts rather than the primary cells the paper sometimes calls them. His verdict is generous: this is a resource paper, and a useful one. It hands other labs a tractable system and a gene list to test — and it validates against real infection data from Marburg-infected rousette spleens rather than standing alone. Rabies shots cost $11,000 to $14,000 — and exposures are up 17% A CDC health alert reports a nationwide rise in reported human rabies exposures and post-exposure treatment. From July through August 2026, the CDC fielded 17% more rabies-related inquiries than in the same period of 2025, including mass exposure events involving more than one person. A typical post-exposure course runs $11,000 to $14,000. The hosts use a listener question — from two Minnesota veterinarians whose clients refuse to vaccinate their pets — to walk through the economics. If a rabid pet bites someone, the owner faces serious financial liability, not just the prophylaxis bill. Dog rabies vaccination is legally required in every state the hosts have lived in, with a tag as proof; unvaccinated, unlicensed dogs can be confiscated and euthanized. The human vaccine is inactivated virus; the pet vaccine is a poxvirus-vectored rabies glycoprotein, commonly canarypox, given annually or every other year. The old painful abdominal series is gone. Condit's bottom line: the disease is effectively 100% fatal once symptoms appear, so there is no reason to gamble. And the gamble isn't only the owner's — it's the neighbor who gets bitten. Measles won't escape the vaccine, so don't run the experiment A listener asks whether rampant measles in under-vaccinated populations could select a variant that defeats the current vaccine. The short answer is probably not, and the reasoning is elegant. Measles is monotypic — one strain worldwide, as far as anyone knows — and the vaccine has stayed effective for roughly six decades. People who survived natural infection were immune for life, which is what made a vaccine plausible in the first place. The explanation is fitness cost. Racaniello recalls a paper in which the measles glycoprotein was mutated up and down: some regions tolerate change, others cannot — analogous to an aircraft returning from battle with damage concentrated where it matters least. Influenza's hemagglutinin has more room to tinker around the active site, and its segmented genome plus avian reservoir make antigenic variation a different problem entirely. Dove offers a fitness-landscape analogy: adaptation is like climbing out of a gravity well, and measles sits in a deep one. The hosts note they asked an AI, which agreed there are no known antibody-escape mutants, then joked it may simply have mined their own conversation. Condit's verdict: a damn interesting question, and still not a good experiment to run. Trust in science fell to 72% — and it tracks inequality The Wellcome Global Monitor 2026, "Trust in Science Under Pressure," draws on 140,000 adults across 140 countries — the largest study of public trust in science. Three findings stand out: trust has fallen since the COVID-19 pandemic; trust is associated with stronger, more equal societies; and trust is higher among people who see science as relevant and beneficial to them. Measure 2018 2020 2025 Report some or a lot of trust in science 77% 80% 72% Trust in science has fallen more than trust in other institutions, and low-trust groups are further apart from everyone else in their attitudes. The country-level picture is stark: Finland tops the chart with 66% high trust and 76% saying science benefits most people; Somalia sits at the bottom with 9%, alongside Congo, Ecuador, Albania, and Peru. The US lands at 53% high trust and 57% on benefit — higher than the hosts expected. Racaniello attributes part of the decline to visible anti-science actors, particularly the anti-vaccine movement, and part to a perception that public health overreached during COVID. Dove counters that people at the bottom of the chart are dealing with more immediate dangers, and that much of what is bad in their lives also comes from science. The relevance to everything above is direct. Surveillance, vaccination, and culling are all public acts. They require a public that trusts the institutions asking. Health care ranks last at 4% Racaniello opens the political segment with a New York Times poll by Echelon Insights of voters who backed Trump in 2024 and no longer support him. Cost of living tops the list at 42%. Immigration sits at 5%, democracy at 6%, and health care dead last at 4%. His argument: health care is being trashed — the CDC, infectious disease tracking, science funding — and there is a measles outbreak that should not exist. Dove's reading is that the question forced a single biggest issue, and someone three months behind on rent will name rent. The exchange turns to constitutional safeguards. Dove notes the framers built checks against a demagogue but did not anticipate an entire party going along; Condit notes they assumed rational, well-informed negotiators. Dove plugs the PBS NewsHour for putting people of diverse views into actual discussion, and argues that well-informed coverage tilts left because it tries to be reality-based. Four dollars of cardboard, four days instead of two weeks The episode ends somewhere unexpectedly practical. Condit's pick, passed along by his wife: a PLOS ONE randomized controlled trial titled "The effect of a hiding box on stress levels and body weight in Dutch shelter cats." Twenty-three cats newly arrived at a shelter were assigned a cardboard box or not. Body weight was unaffected — all cats lose weight while adjusting. But on a structured stress rubric covering posture and ear position, cats with boxes adapted in about four days versus roughly two weeks without. The mechanism is concealment and security. Condit connects it to his own cat's boarding experience at a purpose-built cattery: a large room with floor-to-ceiling mesh enclosures, cat trees, windows, and daily photos. The first two days of photos reproducibly showed the cat hiding in a box in the cat tree; after that he came out to play. Dove notes the behavior isn't domestic-cat-specific — his local zoo's bobcats curl up in Amazon boxes. Dove's pick is Edward Gorey's Fantod Pack, a tarot-style deck of about 20 cards in the artist's dark Victorian line style, timed for Halloween and the gift season. Racaniello's pick is the Wellcome Global Monitor itself. A listener recommends Michael Lewis's Who Is Government? and Blockers, the latter covering DOGE, Project 2025, and the removal of experienced civil servants, including a chapter on Francis Collins trying to determine who forced him out. What to watch The unresolved tension is between what the sequences show and what the surveillance system can see. The Utah mink cluster has a single introduction, a known date, and a shared mutation — PB1 K388R — that has now appeared in mammals at least twice. But the intermediate host, the feed source, and any nearby infected herds remain unidentified, and no samples have been taken since the first week of August. The same blind spot applies to cattle in Kansas and Washington, where H5N1 has been detected but never sequenced. For anyone thinking about risk rather than just reading about it, the message is uncomfortable: the systems that would catch a pandemic early are being switched off, not because the science failed but because the funding, compensation, and political will behind them failed. news.content_original: Ask AIReal-time News Market Earnings CallEvent Calendar More Earnings CallEvent CalendarWatchlistPodcastMarket InfluencersMore Ask AIReal-time News WatchlistHoldingsMarketEarnings CallEvent CalendarPodcastMarket Influencers Utah Mink Outbreak: Virologists Say H5N1 Slipped From Cattle While USDA Watched 2026-11-01 05:08 (GMT+0) Add preferred source An H5N1 outbreak in Utah mink has been traced genetically to the cattle-adapted B3.13 strain now circulating in US dairy herds — not to wild birds — revealing a virus that moved undetected for roughly six weeks and a surveillance system that has since stopped looking. Analysis of the outbreak preprint on the virology podcast TWiV, by hosts Rich Condit and Alan Dove alongside Vincent Racaniello, makes the case that the largest risk isn't the mink themselves but what their infection implies: each new mammalian host is another roll of the dice toward human adaptation. The same episode contrasts this with Marburg virus, where a Cell Reports study explains why the virus is harmless in its bat reservoir but lethal in people — bats mount a narrow, restrained antiviral response while humans trigger broad inflammatory damage. The report also covers rising rabies exposure costs, why measles is unlikely to escape its vaccine, and a global survey showing trust in science fell from 80% in 2020 to 72% in 2025. For investors, the through-line is that underfunded surveillance and eroding public trust are themselves systemic risks in any pandemic-exposed portfolio. Key Elements H5N1USDAUtah mink farmB3.13 genotypeMarburg virusCell ReportsGustavo PalaciosAlvin CrespoThomas PeacockWellcome Global MonitorCDCEgyptian rousette batPLOS ONEPirbright Institute Something is moving H5N1 between American farms, and the people whose job it is to track it have stopped taking samples. In August 2026, USDA inspectors collected swabs from captive mink at a farm in Salt Lake County, Utah. The virus they found was not the bird flu that arrives each season with wild waterfowl. Genetically, all ten whole-genome sequences the team analyzed belonged to B3.13 — the cattle-adapted lineage that first appeared in Texas dairy herds in March 2024 — according to a preprint discussed by virologists Rich Condit and Alan Dove on the podcast This Week in Virology. The mink outbreak matters because of what it tells us about the virus's staying power. "The longer the virus spends in mammals, the better the chances we think that it will be able to adapt to humans and establish human-to-human spread," Dove said. Cattle and mink are two very different mammals. A virus that can jump between them is a virus testing new furniture in the house. A six-week head start, and one mutation to watch The epidemiological timeline is the story here. Genetic analysis places the most recent common ancestor of the Utah mink cluster at July 4, 2026. The samples weren't collected until August 7, and detection was confirmed ten days later. That means the virus circulated in the mink sheds for roughly six weeks before anyone looked. By September 29, the outbreak was reportedly still ongoing — and no further samples had been taken after that first batch. The sequences point to a single introduction, followed by diversification. Ten genomes, one cluster, all nested inside the 2026 B3.13 cattle group alongside strains from Idaho, Texas, and Utah dairy herds. One shared mutation, PB1 K388R, appears in every mink virus — a change rarely seen in wild birds but previously documented in Spanish mink infected in October 2022. The viruses also carry PB2 M631L, a cattle mutation known to boost replication in mammals. Finding Detail Genotype B3.13, the cattle-adapted clade first seen in Texas in March 2024 Cluster structure Single introduction, then diversification — all 10 sequences in one cluster Estimated entry into mink July 4, 2026 (most recent common ancestor) Detection August 17, 2026; samples from August 7 Shared mutation PB1 K388R in all 10 mink viruses; previously seen in Spanish mink, October 2022 Pre-existing cattle mutations PB2 M631L (increases replication in mammals); neuraminidase changes linked to earlier mink outbreaks Closest relatives Texas cattle strains sampled May 2026, with a three-month gap How the virus traveled from Texas cattle to Utah mink is unknown — and the authors are candid about it. Their candidate list: shared workers, vehicles or equipment moving between farms, or feed. Mink are carnivores, often fed poultry products that travel long distances across state lines. Farm labor is precarious and mobile. "Our inability to pinpoint the source of the Utah outbreak points to large surveillance gaps for highly pathogenic avian influenza in US livestock," the authors wrote, as read by host Vincent Racaniello. The gaps run deeper than one farm. H5N1 has been detected in dairy cattle in Kansas and Washington, but no sequences exist for those herds, so their relationship to the Utah cluster is unknown. There may be unidentified infected herds near the mink farm. Utah and Idaho are two of the largest mink-producing states, and both have continuing B3.13 circulation in cattle — a coincidence the preprint's authors treat as a risk factor. The policy problem is the real outbreak Here is where the science meets the politics, and where the hosts don't hold back. By the preprint's account, neither the state nor the USDA ordered culling or monitored exposed farm workers. The USDA told the state veterinarian there was no mechanism to authorize vaccination or to compensate the producer for mink losses. Alleged fur-industry pressure has discouraged regulation. Federal interstate testing requirements apply to lactating dairy cattle, yet the virus keeps shuttling between Idaho, Texas, and Utah. Dove pushes back on the easy explanation that a different administration would simply test more. He argues the USDA has a structural conflict baked into its mission — promoting agriculture on one side, protecting public health on the other — and that farm margins are razor thin. Any intervention carries real cost and real political resistance. Poultry culling happens because export markets demand it. There is no comparable export pressure for mink pelts: 80% of the farmed mink market is in China, which means US producers have almost no domestic demand to protect — and little industry-side incentive to fund surveillance or accept a cull. Why mink in particular? "Mink could be a vessel for reassortment between human and avian strains," Condit said. Farmed mink are one of the few settings where a human-adapted influenza virus might meet a bird-adapted one inside the same animal. The preprint's own open questions read like a to-do list nobody has picked up: will the virus spread to other mink farms (SARS-CoV-2 spread across six Utah mink farms in 2020, possibly via free-roaming cats), is it still adapting to mink, and why haven't wild birds seeded North American mink outbreaks the way gulls did in Spain and Finland? For perspective on severity, consider the baseline. Avian-origin H5N1 kills up to half the people it infects. The cattle-linked B genotype has produced mostly mild human cases; the D genotype has been more severe. "When humans get avian H5N1 from birds it has a high fatality, right up to 50%," Racaniello said. "The cases associated with the B genotype from cows have been mild." The mink viruses belong to the cattle world. That is reassuring today. The question is what six more weeks — or six more months — of unchecked mammalian circulation does to that picture. Why Marburg kills us and leaves bats alone The second paper in the episode answers a question that sounds like trivia but isn't: how does a virus that is lethal to humans live peacefully inside a bat? A study in Cell Reports, led by Gustavo Palacios with co-first authors André Philippe Pastor and Shruti Sherath, compared Egyptian rousette bat cells and human cells to find out. The design was simple: hit fibroblasts with poly(I:C), a synthetic stand-in for double-stranded viral RNA, for four hours, then sequence the RNA and compare what each species switched on. Four functional gene classes emerged — human genes sitting low at baseline, bat genes sitting low at baseline, genes the bats induced strongly, and genes the humans induced strongly. The pattern is the point. Bat cells switched on a tight set of antiviral effectors such as ZBP1 and held inflammatory signals like chemokines and IL-6 in check. Human cells lit up a broad inflammatory and cytokine program plus Toll-like receptors and RIG-I pathway components, along with genes tied to necroptosis and apoptosis. The authors describe the bat response as "robust yet restrained" and the human one as "indiscriminate inflammatory amplification" — the mechanism they suspect drives the cytokine storm that makes Marburg disease so destructive. The hosts repeatedly invoke a warning from a colleague: "if you've seen one bat, you've seen one bat." Bat immunology varies wildly across species — some have a contracted type I interferon locus with constitutive interferon alpha, others have expanded interferon omega genes, some lack interferon alpha entirely. Interferon epsilon gets its own section in the paper: rousette intestinal organoids and airway cultures show elevated constitutive epsilon and interferon-stimulated genes, and a prior study concluded epsilon production drives bat immune resilience. In rousettes, epsilon is highest in brain, ovaries, and liver, absent from most immune tissues, and unchanged after infection — largely mirroring human biology. Condit raises the main methodological caveat, and it's worth hearing because it's how real science gets read. These are dermal fibroblasts — not immune cells, not endothelial cells, and not the epithelial frontline where infection starts. He checked the cell bank records and found the cells are around passage 14, subcultured enough to be effectively pure fibroblasts rather than the primary cells the paper sometimes calls them. His verdict is generous: this is a resource paper, and a useful one. It hands other labs a tractable system and a gene list to test — and it validates against real infection data from Marburg-infected rousette spleens rather than standing alone. Rabies shots cost $11,000 to $14,000 — and exposures are up 17% A CDC health alert reports a nationwide rise in reported human rabies exposures and post-exposure treatment. From July through August 2026, the CDC fielded 17% more rabies-related inquiries than in the same period of 2025, including mass exposure events involving more than one person. A typical post-exposure course runs $11,000 to $14,000. The hosts use a listener question — from two Minnesota veterinarians whose clients refuse to vaccinate their pets — to walk through the economics. If a rabid pet bites someone, the owner faces serious financial liability, not just the prophylaxis bill. Dog rabies vaccination is legally required in every state the hosts have lived in, with a tag as proof; unvaccinated, unlicensed dogs can be confiscated and euthanized. The human vaccine is inactivated virus; the pet vaccine is a poxvirus-vectored rabies glycoprotein, commonly canarypox, given annually or every other year. The old painful abdominal series is gone. Condit's bottom line: the disease is effectively 100% fatal once symptoms appear, so there is no reason to gamble. And the gamble isn't only the owner's — it's the neighbor who gets bitten. Measles won't escape the vaccine, so don't run the experiment A listener asks whether rampant measles in under-vaccinated populations could select a variant that defeats the current vaccine. The short answer is probably not, and the reasoning is elegant. Measles is monotypic — one strain worldwide, as far as anyone knows — and the vaccine has stayed effective for roughly six decades. People who survived natural infection were immune for life, which is what made a vaccine plausible in the first place. The explanation is fitness cost. Racaniello recalls a paper in which the measles glycoprotein was mutated up and down: some regions tolerate change, others cannot — analogous to an aircraft returning from battle with damage concentrated where it matters least. Influenza's hemagglutinin has more room to tinker around the active site, and its segmented genome plus avian reservoir make antigenic variation a different problem entirely. Dove offers a fitness-landscape analogy: adaptation is like climbing out of a gravity well, and measles sits in a deep one. The hosts note they asked an AI, which agreed there are no known antibody-escape mutants, then joked it may simply have mined their own conversation. Condit's verdict: a damn interesting question, and still not a good experiment to run. Trust in science fell to 72% — and it tracks inequality The Wellcome Global Monitor 2026, "Trust in Science Under Pressure," draws on 140,000 adults across 140 countries — the largest study of public trust in science. Three findings stand out: trust has fallen since the COVID-19 pandemic; trust is associated with stronger, more equal societies; and trust is higher among people who see science as relevant and beneficial to them. Measure 2018 2020 2025 Report some or a lot of trust in science 77% 80% 72% Trust in science has fallen more than trust in other institutions, and low-trust groups are further apart from everyone else in their attitudes. The country-level picture is stark: Finland tops the chart with 66% high trust and 76% saying science benefits most people; Somalia sits at the bottom with 9%, alongside Congo, Ecuador, Albania, and Peru. The US lands at 53% high trust and 57% on benefit — higher than the hosts expected. Racaniello attributes part of the decline to visible anti-science actors, particularly the anti-vaccine movement, and part to a perception that public health overreached during COVID. Dove counters that people at the bottom of the chart are dealing with more immediate dangers, and that much of what is bad in their lives also comes from science. The relevance to everything above is direct. Surveillance, vaccination, and culling are all public acts. They require a public that trusts the institutions asking. Health care ranks last at 4% Racaniello opens the political segment with a New York Times poll by Echelon Insights of voters who backed Trump in 2024 and no longer support him. Cost of living tops the list at 42%. Immigration sits at 5%, democracy at 6%, and health care dead last at 4%. His argument: health care is being trashed — the CDC, infectious disease tracking, science funding — and there is a measles outbreak that should not exist. Dove's reading is that the question forced a single biggest issue, and someone three months behind on rent will name rent. The exchange turns to constitutional safeguards. Dove notes the framers built checks against a demagogue but did not anticipate an entire party going along; Condit notes they assumed rational, well-informed negotiators. Dove plugs the PBS NewsHour for putting people of diverse views into actual discussion, and argues that well-informed coverage tilts left because it tries to be reality-based. Four dollars of cardboard, four days instead of two weeks The episode ends somewhere unexpectedly practical. Condit's pick, passed along by his wife: a PLOS ONE randomized controlled trial titled "The effect of a hiding box on stress levels and body weight in Dutch shelter cats." Twenty-three cats newly arrived at a shelter were assigned a cardboard box or not. Body weight was unaffected — all cats lose weight while adjusting. But on a structured stress rubric covering posture and ear position, cats with boxes adapted in about four days versus roughly two weeks without. The mechanism is concealment and security. Condit connects it to his own cat's boarding experience at a purpose-built cattery: a large room with floor-to-ceiling mesh enclosures, cat trees, windows, and daily photos. The first two days of photos reproducibly showed the cat hiding in a box in the cat tree; after that he came out to play. Dove notes the behavior isn't domestic-cat-specific — his local zoo's bobcats curl up in Amazon boxes. Dove's pick is Edward Gorey's Fantod Pack, a tarot-style deck of about 20 cards in the artist's dark Victorian line style, timed for Halloween and the gift season. Racaniello's pick is the Wellcome Global Monitor itself. A listener recommends Michael Lewis's Who Is Government? and Blockers, the latter covering DOGE, Project 2025, and the removal of experienced civil servants, including a chapter on Francis Collins trying to determine who forced him out. What to watch The unresolved tension is between what the sequences show and what the surveillance system can see. The Utah mink cluster has a single introduction, a known date, and a shared mutation — PB1 K388R — that has now appeared in mammals at least twice. But the intermediate host, the feed source, and any nearby infected herds remain unidentified, and no samples have been taken since the first week of August. And the one policy lever that might change the mink outbreak's trajectory — paying producers to cull — has been ruled out as unavailable. analysis.brief_en: In August 2026, an H5N1 outbreak was discovered in mink at a Utah farm, traced genetically to the cattle-adapted B3.13 strain, not wild birds. The virus had been circulating undetected for about six weeks, with the most recent common ancestor dated to July 4, 2026. The outbreak highlights the risk of H5N1 adapting to mammals, potentially leading to human adaptation. The USDA did not implement culling or monitoring of exposed workers, and there is no mechanism for vaccination or compensation for mink losses. The situation underscores the challenges in tracking and responding to highly pathogenic avian influenza in livestock, particularly in the mink farming industry, where there is little incentive for surveillance or intervention due to the lack of domestic demand for mink pelts. The broader implications include the need for improved surveillance and the potential for the virus to evolve into a more severe form if left unchecked in mammalian hosts.

The situation underscores the challenges in tracking and responding to highly pathogenic avian influenza in livestock, particularly in the mink farming industry, where there is little incentive for surveillance or intervention due to the lack of domestic demand for mink pelts. The broader implications include the need for improved surveillance and the potential for the virus to evolve into a more severe form if left unchecked in mammalian hosts.

analysis_zh.time: 暴发 于 2026 年 8 月被发现,通过基因分析确定最近的共同祖先于 2026 年 7 月 4 日,并于 2026 年 8 月 7 日采集了第一批样本。十天后,即 2026 年 8 月 17 日,该检测得到确认。据报道,暴发 于 2026 年 9 月 29 日仍在进行中。(N1、N15、N16、N17、 N18)。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 暴发 事件发生在犹他州,特别是在盐湖县的一个水貂养殖场。受影响的种群包括农场的水貂,它们是食肉动物,经常喂食家禽产品。

This confirmation highlights the ongoing concern about avian influenza in agricultural settings. The article notes that the virus has been identified in the herd, but it does not provide specific details on the number of affected animals, deaths, or the extent of the outbreak. The report also emphasizes the importance of monitoring and managing such outbreaks to protect both livestock and human health. The confirmation was made through official channels, and the article suggests that further actions may be taken to contain the spread of the virus. However, the details of the response and the current status of the outbreak remain unclear based on the supplied evidence.

news.content: 24/7 LiveNew York CityNew JerseyLong IslandNorthern SuburbsConnecticut 71° Bird Flu Washington state resident dies of bird flu after being exposed to infected cattle | What to know The person who died was exposed to infected cattle, officials said. Watch ABC News live news stream and get 24/7 latest, breaking news coverage, and live video. ByMary Kekatos Tuesday, November 3, 2026 5:02PM Share Washington state health officials this week reported what is believed to be the first bird flu death of the year. The person who died was a resident of Yakima County, in south central Washington on the border with Oregon, who was hospitalized with "severe illness," authorities noted. Officials said the person contracted bird flu, also known as avian influenza, following exposure to infected cattle. They had underlying health conditions, according to the Yakima Health District. This colorized electron microscope image shows avian influenza A H5N1 virus particles (yellow), grown in Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) epithelial cells (blue). (CDC/NIAID via AP, File) Public health specialists said the death is a reminder that bird flu is still present and circulating. "While we haven't heard much about it, maybe in the last year or so, the virus has not gone away because there have been periodic detections of this [bird flu] in dairy cattle," Andrew Pekosz, professor and vice chair of the W. Harry Feinstone department of molecular microbiology and immunology at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told ABC News. According to Pekosz, "the sequence of the virus" shows that it has remained active. "It's sort of the same virus that has been around for a couple of years now," he said. "So, this all indicates that the virus continues to spread in dairy cows." Washington state has recorded three cases of bird flu so far this year, all associated with people who either work at dairy farms or were in contact with infected dairy cows, according to local reports. Top Stories Bronx vigil honors murdered 15-year-old student, Javits Frimpong 2 hours ago Cascon Cheesecake in Queens robbed of $40,000 in overnight theft Family seeks answers after 24-year-old found dead in duffel bag in Brooklyn 2 hours ago Pekosz said he agrees with local health officials that the risk to the general public is low and that most people do not need to be concerned. However, he said the death is a reminder to public health officials to be more aware of bird flu viruses. He added that there is also mild concern about bird flu cases in humans being confirmed as seasonal influenza start to spread, arriving early in several parts of the country. Data from the Washington State Department of Health shows that influenza activity in the state is elevated and increasing. Experts have previously said recombination of bird flu and seasonal influenza is unlikely because bird flu is not yet showing evidence of person-to-person transmission. "We need to keep our eye on that because there still is a possibility that this virus could mutate, pick up the genetic capacity to spread readily from human to human," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, told ABC News. "It can't do that at the present time, although it can in ... people with chronic illnesses, such as this person in the state of Washington who unfortunately died of a bird flu illness." Schaffner and Pekosz said this is a reminder for people to get their seasonal influenza vaccine if they have not done so already, and that it's not too late. "Influenza started early in many parts of the country, including my own," Schaffner said. "But remember, flu lasts throughout December into January and into February and even beyond. So, there's plenty of winter to come, during which you want to have as much protection against severe disease that the vaccine can provide." analysis.brief_en: A Washington state resident has died from bird flu after being exposed to infected cattle, marking what health officials believe is the first such death of the year. The individual, who had underlying health conditions, was hospitalized with severe illness in Yakima County, which is located in south central Washington near Oregon. This case is part of a broader trend, as Washington has reported three bird flu cases this year, all linked to people working on or in contact with dairy farms. Public health specialists emphasize that while the risk to the general population remains low, there is a mild concern about potential overlap with seasonal influenza, which has already started to spread in the region. Experts warn that the virus could mutate and gain the ability to spread between humans, but currently, there is no evidence of person-to-person transmission. The death serves as a reminder for people to consider getting their seasonal influenza vaccine, especially as flu activity is elevated and expected to continue through winter.

The death serves as a reminder for people to consider getting their seasonal influenza vaccine, especially as flu activity is elevated and expected to continue through winter.

Photograph: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/AP Washington state resident dies from ‘severe illness’ after contracting bird flu Individual, who also had underlying conditions, was hospitalized after being exposed to avian influenza A Washington state resident has died after being hospitalized with “severe illness” after contracting bird flu, local health officials said on Sunday. The individual was exposed to avian influenza, also known as bird flu, at a dairy with infected cattle in Yakima county, according to a news release. The person was subsequently hospitalized with severe illness and died on Sunday. Health officials said that the individual, whose identity had not been released, had underlying health conditions. “The Yakima health district offers its heartfelt condolences to the individual’s family, friends, and loved ones during this difficult time,” the district said in a statement. This is the first person in the United States to die from complications from bird flu this year, according to the Associated Press. It comes as officials in Yakima county have reported that since early October, 33 dairy herds have tested positive for “highly pathogenic avian influenza”. ‘It’s clear they are under-vaccinated’: Amish under spotlight amid Pennsylvania measles outbreak Read more The Yakima health district has said that it, in coordination with the Washington state department of health, is monitoring human cases of bird flu in Yakima county. So far, the district has recorded three confirmed human cases in the county. In Sunday’s statement, the health district announced the county’s third confirmed human case of bird flu. The individual was “exposed to infected dairy cattle at a Yakima county dairy”, but has not experienced severe illness or required hospitalization. Officials said they are working with public health partners to identify and contact any individuals “who may have been in close contact with the person to monitor for symptoms”. County officials have stressed that “the risk of avian influenza infection to the general public remains low” and that “people at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus”. Human-to-human transmission of bird flu is “extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States”, they said. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has recorded 72 human cases of bird flu across the country since 2024, according to agency data. The CDC has maintained that there is no known person-to-person spread and that the risk to the general public remains low. The CDC announced the first death in the US due to complications from bird flu in January 2025. analysis_en.event: A Washington state resident died after being hospitalized with a severe illness following exposure to avian influenza A H5N1 virus. This is the first death in the US this year from bird flu complications.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: Yakima county has reported 33 dairy herds testing positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza since early October. analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health officials are monitoring human cases and identifying individuals who may have been in close contact with the deceased. The CDC has confirmed no known person-to-person spread of bird flu in the US.

news.source_body_en: A Washington state resident has died after contracting bird flu, marking the first fatality in the US this year from complications of the disease. analysis.time: The Yakima County bird flu death was reported on November 3, 2026, with the event occurring in the context of the ongoing 2026 outbreak. The third dairy-linked human case was confirmed in the same timeframe.
analysis.location_and_population: The event occurred in Yakima County, Washington, United States, involving a county resident exposed to infected dairy cattle. The population affected includes individuals who may have been exposed to the virus through contact with infected animals.
analysis.event: A Yakima County resident died from H5N1 bird flu after exposure to infected dairy cattle, as confirmed by the Yakima Health District and the CDC. This marks the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026 and the third human case linked to dairy cattle since 2024.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: This is the first human death from bird flu in the U.S. this year and the third since the virus was found in dairy cattle in 2024. The CDC confirmed the virus as H5N1, and the individual had underlying health conditions and was hospitalized with severe illness. The spread of the virus among dairy cattle has been reported in Washington state, with 40 herds infected.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Yakima Health District and CDC confirmed the case and death. However, the number of exposed farmworkers tested remains unreported, indicating some uncertainty in the full scope of the outbreak. The situation is under investigation, with ongoing efforts to monitor the spread of the virus.

analysis.brief_en: A Yakima County resident in Washington, United States, has died from H5N1 bird flu after exposure to infected dairy cattle, marking the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026 and the third since the virus was found in dairy cattle in 2024. The Yakima Health District and CDC confirmed the case, noting the individual had underlying health conditions and was hospitalized with severe illness. This death is part of a broader outbreak affecting 40 dairy herds in Washington state, though the number of exposed farmworkers tested remains unreported. The event occurred on November 3, 2026, and the situation is under investigation. The virus is classified as H5N1, a highly pathogenic avian influenza subtype, and its spread among cattle has raised concerns about potential human transmission.

news.source_body_en: A Yakima County resident in Washington, United States, has died from H5N1 bird flu after exposure to infected dairy cattle, marking the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026 and the third since the virus was found in dairy cattle in 2024. The Yakima Health District and CDC confirmed the case, noting the individual had underlying health conditions and was hospitalized with severe illness. This death is part of a broader outbreak affecting 40 dairy herds in Washington state, though the number of exposed farmworkers tested remains unreported. The event occurred on November 3, 2026, and the situation is under investigation. The virus is classified as H5N1, a highly pathogenic avian influenza subtype, and its spread among cattle has raised concerns about potential human transmission.

news.content: JournalArta IDEN · GLOBAL Friday, November 6, 2026 · JakartaS&P 7,353.73 ▼4.36%USD/IDR 18,081 ▲0.06%Subscribe JournalArta Global Edition beyond headlines Indonesia ▾ NewsBusinessTravelCulture Asia ▾ Southeast AsiaEast AsiaSouth Asia World ▾ United StatesEuropeMiddle EastAmericas & Africa Business ▾ CompaniesMacro & PolicyEnergy Markets ▾ StocksCryptoForexCommodities Technology ▾ AIGadgetsApps & SoftwareGaming Sport ▾ FootballCombat SportsBasketballMore Sports Lifestyle ▾ EntertainmentTravelFood & HealthShopping & Deals Search Advertisement Discover more Get Cold Relief Check Symptoms Study Biology Manage Livestock Dairy Cattle dairy cows dairy cattle Get Fresh Dairy death Death Lifestyle Lifestyle · Food & Health Third U.S. Bird Flu Death Since Virus Spread to Dairy Cattle A Yakima County resident has died after contracting H5N1 bird flu following exposure to infected dairy cattle, marking the third U.S. death linked to the Check Symptoms By Alistair Sterling November 3, 20262 min read Third U.S. Bird Flu Death Since Virus Spread to Dairy Cattle A Yakima County resident has died after contracting H5N1 bird flu following exposure to infected dairy cattle, marking the third U.S. death linked to the virus since it began spreading among livestock. Health officials say the risk to the wider public remains low. Check Symptoms Discover more Shop Bird Supplies birds health The person, who had underlying health conditions, was hospitalized and died Sunday, the Yakima Health District said. The death is the first in the United States from bird flu complications in 2026. Officials did not release the person’s name. Human infections in Washington The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified the virus as H5N1. Washington health officials have reported three human infections in Yakima County since the virus was found in dairy cattle in the state. The latest case involved someone exposed to dairy cattle and was not described as a severe illness. Check Symptoms Avian influenza viruses mainly circulate among birds, but the H5 strain spread to dairy cows in 2024. Most reported U.S. human infections have involved people who worked on farms with infected cattle or poultry, and officials have characterized most illnesses as mild. Advertisement Discover more Find Grief Support deaths bird There have been two other U.S. deaths since the outbreak became a public health concern: an elderly person in Louisiana who died in 2025 after infection with H5N1, and a Washington resident who died that November from the rarer H5N5 strain. Check Symptoms Public risk remains low Yakima County officials said 33 dairy herds had recently tested positive for H5N1. The district’s health officer, Dr. Dave Atteberry, said the virus can cause serious illness, particularly in people with existing health problems, while stressing that the risk to the general public remains low. The deaths and new infections are being monitored by health officials as the virus continues to be detected in cattle. The CDC has recorded more than 70 human bird flu cases in the United States since 2024. news.source_body_en: A Yakima County resident in Washington, U.S., has died after contracting H5N1 bird flu following exposure to infected dairy cattle, marking the third U.S. death linked to the virus since it began spreading among livestock. The individual, who had underlying health conditions, was hospitalized and died on Sunday, November 6, 2026. This death is the first in the U.S. from bird flu complications in 2026. Health officials have stated that the risk to the general public remains low, though the virus can cause serious illness in people with existing health problems. The CDC confirmed the virus as H5N1, and the deaths and new infections are being monitored as the virus continues to be detected in cattle. Officials did not release the person’s name, and the outbreak is part of a broader trend of H5N1 cases in the U.S. since 2024, with over 70 human cases recorded.
