HAT Radio Stations Contact Us About HAT Advertise with HAT H5N1 Hits Indiana Dairy Farms: 2 Newton County Herds Quarantined as Statewide Restrictions Take Effect by C.J. Miller November 2, 2026 Photo: C.J. Miller / Hoosier Ag Today. Hoosier dairy producers are on high alert following the confirmation of the H5N1 influenza virus in two operationally connected dairy herds in Newton County in northwestern Indiana. The detection officially strips Indiana of its “unaffected state” status and triggers immediate mandatory movement restrictions, farm quarantines, and a 10-kilometer surveillance buffer zone near the affected farms. The initial detection did not originate from clinical signs on the farm, but through routine National Milk Testing Strategy (NMTS) bulk-tank surveillance at an out-of-state dairy processing facility. After the virus was flagged in a holding silo receiving Indiana milk, the Indiana State Board of Animal Health (BOAH) collected follow-up samples at the source farms. The tests were confirmed positive by the Indiana Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (ADDL) and verified by the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL) in Ames, Iowa. When pressed on where the processing facility is located, BOAH officials declined to identify the specific state of origin, stating that state health officials and veterinarians in that jurisdiction are still actively investigating epidemiological links and contacting partners before details are made public. For Indiana’s 660 dairy operations—which together produce more than 4.51 billion pounds of milk annually—the regulatory landscape has immediately shifted. Indiana is now the 21st state in the U.S. where a positive case of H5N1 has been detected in dairy cattle. Mandatory Interstate Testing & Herd Status Options Under USDA federal orders, any lactating dairy cow or dairy-beef cross leaving Indiana must now test negative for H5N1 prior to interstate movement. Private herd veterinarians must collect individual animal samples for testing through the ADDL or accredited diagnostic facilities before shipment paperwork can be cleared. To bypass individual animal testing delays and reduce paperwork for high-frequency shippers, BOAH is urging regular interstate exporters to enroll in the USDA Dairy Herd Status Program. “Under a normal movement, every individual animal needs to be tested before that lactating dairy cow can move across state lines,” explained Denise Derrer Spears, Public Information Officer for BOAH. “If the herd is tested on a weekly basis, that establishes a status for all the animals in that herd, and therefore they can just make the movement as needed.” Producers interested in enrolling in the voluntary program should contact BOAH at animalhealth@boah.in.gov or work directly with their herd veterinarian. Quarantine Protocol & The 10-km Surveillance Zone For the two infected dairies in Newton County, strict quarantine orders are in effect for all lactating cattle. Under BOAH’s emergency response plan, farm-level testing will continue weekly until the herds achieve two consecutive negative bulk-tank tests, at which point the quarantine will be lifted. The impact extends well beyond the two affected operations. BOAH has established an active 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) Surveillance Zone around the infected sites. All Grade A dairy farms and commercial poultry facilities located within this 10-km perimeter are subject to mandatory community spread verification. Surveillance testing within the zone will be conducted every 28 days until the quarantined farms complete their clearance protocols. To assist with wildlife vectors, USDA Wildlife Services and the Indiana Department of Natural Resources (DNR) are conducting active wild bird surveillance in and around the Newton County surveillance perimeter. Wild waterfowl were identified as the primary catalyst when H5N1 first crossed into U.S. dairy cattle in Texas back in March 2024. Biosecurity Focus: Transmission Routes Between Operations Epidemiological investigations into H5N1 outbreaks across the Midwest—including USDA findings from Michigan’s 2024 dairy event—reveal that disease spread between dairies is rarely driven by live animal additions. Instead, transmission occurs through indirect operational links: shared personnel, contract haulers, deadstock pickup, feed deliveries, and unpasteurized milk transport. Because the two Newton County herds were described as operationally connected, BOAH is warning neighboring farms and connected operations to audit every daily off-farm traffic point. “Really, what it gets down to when it comes to biosecurity, the basics are really, really important: clean hands, clean feet, clean vehicles,” Spears emphasized. “Cleaning your hands and feet before you get in and out of a truck, a tractor, or any type of vehicle on and off of those farms is really important, especially before going to the next farm.” Spears cautioned producers against viewing biosecurity as a seasonal task. “Biosecurity is really important, and that’s 365 days a year,” Spears said. “You can’t just think, ‘Oh, it’s high-path flu season,’ and just do it now. It can happen to anybody, anytime, and it just really emphasizes—regardless of the species or the type of operation—clean hands, clean feet, clean equipment.” Because the H5N1 virus is heavily concentrated in raw, unpasteurized milk, BOAH stresses that equipment, tires, and footwear exposed to parlor wash water or raw milk must be thoroughly disinfected before leaving any facility. Consumer Confidence & Herd Monitoring State health and agricultural officials reiterate that the discovery presents no food safety threat to the public. Commercial pasteurization effectively inactivates the H5N1 virus, and pasteurized milk, eggs, beef, and poultry remain completely safe for consumers. However, pet owners are advised against feeding uncooked diets or raw milk to household animals, as domestic cats are highly susceptible to severe H5N1 clinical illness. Producers across Indiana should closely monitor cattle for hallmark symptoms, including: Sudden drop in herd-wide milk production Tacky, thickened, or colostrum-like milk consistency Decreased feed intake and rumen motility Diarrhea, lethargy, dehydration, and fever If clinical signs appear, cattle owners should isolate affected animals and contact their herd veterinarian immediately. For real-time updates on Indiana’s H5N1 dashboard, surveillance status, and e-newsletter alerts, visit the Indiana State Board of Animal Health website at in.gov/boah. HAT Radio Stations Contact Us About HAT Advertise with HAT H5N1 Hits Indiana Dairy Farms: 2 Newton County Herds Quarantined as Statewide Restrictions Take Effect by C.J. Miller November 2, 2026 Photo: C.J. Miller / Hoosier Ag Today. Hoosier dairy producers are on high alert following the confirmation of the H5N1 influenza virus in two operationally connected dairy herds in Newton County in northwestern Indiana. The detection officially strips Indiana of its “unaffected state” status and triggers immediate mandatory movement restrictions, farm quarantines, and a 10-kilometer surveillance buffer zone near the affected farms. The initial detection did not originate from clinical signs on the farm, but through routine National Milk Testing Strategy (NMTS) bulk-tank surveillance at an out-of-state dairy processing facility. After the virus was flagged in a holding silo receiving Indiana milk, the Indiana State Board of Animal Health (BOAH) collected follow-up samples at the source farms. The tests were confirmed positive by the Indiana Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (ADDL) and verified by the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL) in Ames, Iowa. When pressed on where the processing facility is located, BOAH officials declined to identify the specific state of origin, stating that state health officials and veterinarians in that jurisdiction are still actively investigating epidemiological links and contacting partners before details are made public. For Indiana’s 660 dairy operations—which together produce more than 4.51 billion pounds of milk annually—the regulatory landscape has immediately shifted. Indiana is now the 21st state in the U.S. where a positive case of H5N1 has been detected in dairy cattle. Mandatory Interstate Testing & Herd Status Options Under USDA federal orders, any lactating dairy cow or dairy-beef cross leaving Indiana must now test negative for H5N1 prior to interstate movement. Private herd veterinarians must collect individual animal samples for testing through the ADDL or accredited diagnostic facilities before shipment paperwork can be cleared. To bypass individual animal testing delays and reduce paperwork for high-frequency shippers, BOAH is urging regular interstate exporters to enroll in the USDA Dairy Herd Status Program. “Under a normal movement, every individual animal needs to be tested before that lactating dairy cow can move across state lines,” explained Denise Derrer Spears, Public Information Officer for BOAH. “If the herd is tested on a weekly basis, that establishes a status for all the animals in that herd, and therefore they can just make the movement as needed.” Producers interested in enrolling in the voluntary program should contact BOAH at animalhealth@boah.in.gov or work directly with their herd veterinarian. Quarantine Protocol & The 10-km Surveillance Zone For the two infected dairies in Newton County, strict quarantine orders are in effect for all lactating cattle. Under BOAH’s emergency response plan, farm-level testing will continue weekly until the herds achieve two consecutive negative bulk-tank tests, at which point the quarantine will be lifted. The impact extends well beyond the two affected operations. BOAH has established an active 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) Surveillance Zone around the infected sites. All Grade A dairy farms and commercial poultry facilities located within this 10-km perimeter are subject to mandatory community spread verification. Surveillance testing within the zone will be conducted every 28 days until the quarantined farms complete their clearance protocols. To assist with wildlife vectors, USDA Wildlife Services and the Indiana Department of Natural Resources (DNR) are conducting active wild bird surveillance in and around the Newton County surveillance perimeter. Wild waterfowl were identified as the primary catalyst when H5N1 first crossed into U.S. dairy cattle in Texas back in March 2024. Biosecurity Focus: Transmission Routes Between Operations Epidemiological investigations into H5N1 outbreaks across the Midwest—including USDA findings from Michigan’s 2024 dairy event—reveal that disease spread between dairies is rarely driven by live animal additions. Instead, transmission occurs through indirect operational links: shared personnel, contract haulers, deadstock pickup, feed deliveries, and unpasteurized milk transport. Because the two Newton County herds were described as operationally connected, BOAH is warning neighboring farms and connected operations to audit every daily off-farm traffic point. “Really, what it gets down to when it comes to biosecurity, the basics are really, really important: clean hands, clean feet, clean vehicles,” Spears emphasized. “Cleaning your hands and feet before you get in and out of a truck, a tractor, or any type of vehicle on and off of those farms is really important, especially before going to the next farm.” Spears cautioned producers against viewing biosecurity as a seasonal task. “Biosecurity is really important, and that’s 365 days a year,” Spears said. “You can’t just think, ‘Oh, it’s high-path flu season,’ and just do it now. It can happen to anybody, anytime, and it just really emphasizes—regardless of the species or the type of operation—clean hands, clean feet, clean equipment.” Because the H5N1 virus is heavily concentrated in raw, unpasteurized milk, BOAH stresses that equipment, tires, and footwear exposed to parlor wash water or raw milk must be thoroughly disinfected before leaving any facility. Consumer Confidence & Herd Monitoring State health and agricultural officials reiterate that the discovery presents no food safety threat to the public. Commercial pasteurization effectively inactivates the H5N1 virus, and pasteurized milk, eggs, beef, and poultry remain completely safe for consumers. However, pet owners are advised against feeding uncooked diets or raw milk to household animals, as domestic cats are highly susceptible to severe H5N1 clinical illness. Producers across Indiana should closely monitor cattle for hallmark symptoms, including: Sudden drop in herd-wide milk production Tacky, thickened, or colostrum-like milk consistency Decreased feed intake and rumen motility Diarrhea, lethargy, dehydration, and fever If clinical signs appear, cattle owners should isolate affected animals and contact their herd veterinarian immediately. For real-time updates on Indiana’s H5N1 dashboard, surveillance status, and e-newsletter alerts, visit the Indiana State Board of Animal Health website at in.gov/boah. news.content: 新闻 体育 汽车 房产 旅游 教育 时尚 科技 财经 娱乐 美国华盛顿州出现禽流感死亡病例,我们需要对此感到恐慌吗? |#科学资讯# #医学# #H5N1禽流感# 2026-11-03 06:02 来源: 常识技能百宝箱 近期,美国华盛顿州卫生部门报告了一起令人关注的公共卫生事件:一名患有基础疾病的居民在接触了受感染的奶牛后,不幸感染了高致病性禽流感(Avian Influenza),并最终导致死亡。这是自2024年以来,美国境内记录的第三例与该病毒相关的死亡病例。 什么是H5N1禽流感? 这次事件的核心对象是H5N1型禽流感病毒。从生物学角度看,这是一种主要在鸟类中传播的病毒,但近年来,它展现出了跨物种传播的能力,开始在部分哺乳动物(如奶牛)中出现感染迹象。约翰斯·霍普金斯大学(Johns Hopkins University)彭博公共卫生学院的安德鲁·佩科斯(Andrew Pekosz)教授指出,这类病毒的跨物种溢出效应是当前公共卫生领域监测的重点。 为什么这起病例值得关注? 在华盛顿州近期发现的三例人类感染病例中,这起死亡事件显得尤为突出。科学家们关注的重点在于,病毒是否在哺乳动物之间发生了变异,从而增强了对人类的潜在威胁。目前,卫生部门正在对相关病例进行流行病学调查,以确定病毒的具体传播链条,并评估是否存在社区传播的风险。 我们需要保持怎样的科学态度? 面对此类新闻,公众容易产生焦虑,但我们需要保持冷静的科学判断。首先,目前所有的证据都指向该患者是在接触受感染奶牛的过程中被传染的,这属于典型的“人畜共患”路径,而非人际间的广泛传播。其次,该患者本身患有基础健康状况,这在医学上是影响病毒感染后果的重要变量,不能简单地将个案的严重性等同于病毒对普通健康人群的普遍威胁。 还有哪些不确定性? 现阶段的证据显示,虽然H5N1病毒在农场动物中的存在是一个明确的科学事实,但它是否会进一步演化出更易在人与人之间传播的特征,目前尚无定论。科研人员正在密切监测病毒的基因序列变化,以寻找任何可能增强其致病性或传播力的突变。在更多深入的分子微生物学研究结果出炉之前,任何过度解读或恐慌都是没有必要的。 总结来说,公共卫生监测的意义在于防患于未然。我们应当关注官方发布的卫生建议,避免接触病死动物,并保持良好的个人卫生习惯。科学的应对之道,永远是基于严谨的数据监测,而非盲目的猜测。 我是胡博士,胡说八道的胡,但胡博士科普向来严谨。欢迎关注,欢迎捉虫。 返回搜狐,查看更多 阅读 () 作者声明 含AI生成内容 平台声明 该文观点仅代表作者本人,搜狐号系信息发布平台,搜狐仅提供信息存储空间服务。

analysis.brief_en: A resident in Washington State, USA, with a pre-existing health condition, died after contracting highly pathogenic avian influenza from an infected cow. This is the third reported case of human infection with the H5N1 virus in the U.S. since 2024. Public health officials are investigating the transmission chain and assessing the risk of community spread. Scientists are monitoring genetic changes in the virus to understand its potential for further adaptation.

USDA-APHIS November 3, 2026 schedule2 Min Read The U.S. Department of Agriculture-Animal & Plant Health Inspection Service’s National Veterinary Services Laboratories confirmed via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 genotype B3.13 in a dairy cattle herd in Indiana. This detection was a result of routine National Milk Testing Strategy testing, not pre-movement surveillance. This marks the first reported case of HPAI in cattle in Indiana. While dairy cattle in a total of 21 states have been infected since the start of the outbreak in March 2024, APHIS has seen cases in previously unaffected states this year. APHIS is working closely with the Indiana State Board of Animal Health to conduct additional on-farm investigations, diagnostic testing and epidemiological data collection to better understand the detection and prevent further disease spread. The detection does not change USDA’s HPAI eradication strategy. Biosecurity is still key to mitigating the risk of disease introduction or spread between premises. APHIS recommends enhanced biosecurity measures for all dairy farms. Producers should immediately report any livestock with clinical signs, or any unusual sick or dead wildlife, to their state veterinarian. Related:IgG levels tracked in dairy calves fed colostrum replacer This detection does not pose a risk to consumer health or affect the safety of the commercial milk supply. The U.S. Food & Drug Administration is confident that pasteurization is effective at inactivating HPAI virus and that the commercial, pasteurized milk supply is safe. Dairies are required to send milk only from healthy animals into processing for human consumption; milk from impacted animals is being diverted from the commercial milk tank or destroyed so that it does not enter the human food supply. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control & Prevention, HPAI viruses circulating in birds and U.S. dairy cattle pose a low risk to the general public in the U.S. However, people who have job-related or recreational exposures to infected birds or mammals are at higher risk of infection and should take appropriate precautions outlined in CDC guidance. Photo by Freek Wolsnik, Pexels. News Release NEWTON COUNTY – Indiana has lost its bird flu-free status for dairy cattle after highly pathogenic avian influenza, H5N1, was confirmed in two connected dairy operations in Newton County, prompting state officials to impose movement restrictions and expand surveillance. The infections were identified through routine milk monitoring under a national surveillance program rather than reports of visibly sick cattle. Veterinarians and disease investigators traced the detection to milk samples flagged by a processing system. Follow-up testing by state and federal laboratories confirmed the virus. Affected herds must remain under movement restrictions until they meet testing requirements, including repeated negative results. Dairy farms and commercial poultry operations within a 10-kilometer perimeter of the infected facilities also will undergo recurring surveillance testing. Indiana now joins other states with confirmed H5N1 infections in dairy cattle. Federal requirements for interstate livestock movements have increased, and state officials are encouraging producers who regularly transport lactating cows across state lines to participate in a herd-status certification program. Producers are being urged to strengthen year-round biosecurity, monitor cattle for reduced milk production, fever, dehydration and changes in behavior, and isolate animals showing symptoms while consulting veterinarians. Wildlife specialists also are monitoring nearby bird populations, particularly migratory waterfowl, which have been associated with previous outbreaks. Officials said commercially processed milk and properly handled beef, poultry and eggs remain safe for consumption. However, raw milk poses potential risks, and pet owners are being cautioned against feeding cats raw milk or uncooked animal products because of their vulnerability to severe H5N1 illness. news.content_zh: 2026 年 11 月 4 日,印第安纳州确认牛顿县两家相连的奶牛场存在 高致病性禽流感 (H5N1),这标志着该州奶牛失去了无禽流感状态。该病毒是通过国家 监测 计划下的常规牛奶监测发现的,而不是通过牛的明显患病迹象发现的。这促使州政府官员对受影响的牛群实施行动限制,并扩大 监测 的努力。方圆10公里内的奶牛场和商业家禽养殖场也正在反复测试。联邦对州际牲畜运输的要求有所提高,并鼓励生产者参与畜群状况认证计划。官员们表示,商业加工的牛奶和妥善处理的动物产品仍然是安全的,但生奶存在潜在风险。建议宠物主人避免给猫喂食生奶或未煮熟的动物产品,因为它们容易感染严重的 H5N1 疾病。野生动物专家正在监测附近的鸟类种群,特别是迁徙水禽,这些鸟类与之前的 暴发 有关。此次检测凸显了生物安全措施和正在进行的 监测 在防止 禽流感 传播方面的重要性。

Coli Tied to Pumpkin Patch Selma Blair on Flight Incident: 'I Am So Sorry' Tailors and Cobblers Are Loving the Ozempic Boom Those Pot Gummies May Not Help You Sleep Like You Think Judge Rejects Medicaid Rule Defining 'Medically Frail' Oscar-Nominated Actor Dies in Assisted Suicide at 95 Health | bird flu Washington State Resident Dies From Bird Flu Person dies from avian influenza following exposure to infected cattle By Newser Editors and Wire Services Posted Nov 3, 2026 1:30 AM CST Copied This colorized electron microscope image released by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases on March 26, 2024, shows avian influenza A H5N1 virus particles (yellow), grown in Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) epithelial cells (blue). (CDC/NIAID via AP, File) A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such US death in a year, the AP reports. The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said. Two other US deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5. Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1. County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1. They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms. The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday. There is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says. Read These Next Witnesses to Indiana execution describe an unusual scene. (CDC/NIAID via AP, File) A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such US death in a year, the AP reports. The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said. Two other US deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5. Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1. County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1. They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms. The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday. There is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says. Read These Next Witnesses to Indiana execution describe an unusual scene. In a news release issued on Sunday, the health district said the person died “today” from complications of avian influenza, also known as bird flu. The health district said the victim had underlying health conditions. “Out of respect for the family’s privacy,” the district said it is not releasing the person’s name, gender or age. Health officials said the risk of avian influenza infection to the general public remains low, but noted that people at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus. The health district said transmission of avian influenza between humans is “extremely rare” and “has never been documented in the United States.” Public health officials are continuing to monitor people who had close contact with the patient for symptoms, the district said. The health district said it is working with public health partners to identify and contact people who may have been in close contact with the individual to monitor for symptoms. news.title_original: Avian influenza spread beyond a backyard coop on an Illinois farm, analysis finds

analysis.time: An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza virus that nearly wiped out an Illinois farmer's backyard flock also spread to a domestic cat and wild rats on the farm, an analysis of the animals by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory found.
analysis.location_and_population: Illinois farm, domestic cat, wild rats.
analysis.event: An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza virus was found to have spread beyond a backyard coop to a domestic cat and wild rats on the farm, according to an analysis by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak nearly wiped out the farmer's backyard flock, with the virus spreading to a domestic cat and wild rats. The scale of impact is limited to the farm, and no explicit risk level was stated in the evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The spread of the virus to non-avian hosts was identified through analysis by the mentioned laboratories. The status of the outbreak is confirmed based on the findings, but no further details on response measures or containment efforts were provided.

Director and executive compensation totalled A$3.27 million, up from A$2.9 million. According to the report, the increase in key management personnel compensation is mostly due to termination benefits associated with the executive team restructure. In August, Dairy Australia confirmed it was reviewing its organisational structure, which was expected to result in redundancies. Staff numbers stood at 180 (169.6 full-time equivalent), down from 186 (171.6) a year earlier. news.source_body_en: On November 3, 2026, Indiana confirmed the first H5N1 infections in two connected dairy herds, according to Dairynews.today. This marks a significant development in the context of avian influenza A viruses, which are the target of the analysis. The report highlights the presence of H5N1 in these herds, indicating a potential risk to the dairy industry. However, no specific case or death counts were provided, and details on testing, isolation, or contact tracing measures remain unclear. The confirmation suggests that the infection is actively being investigated, but further information is needed to fully understand the scale and impact of the outbreak. The report does not mention any broader implications or responses from health authorities, leaving the situation as unresolved with ongoing monitoring.
news.content_zh: 据《今日乳业新闻》报道,2026 年 11 月 3 日,印第安纳州确认两个相连的奶牛场首次出现 H5N1 感染。这标志着作为分析目标的 禽流感 A 病毒的重大发展。该报告强调了这些牛群中存在 H5N1 病毒,表明乳制品行业存在潜在风险。然而,没有提供具体病例或死亡人数,有关检测、隔离或接触者追踪措施的细节仍不清楚。该确认表明正在积极调查该感染,但需要进一步的信息来充分了解 暴发 的规模和影响。该报告没有提及卫生当局的任何更广泛的影响或应对措施,导致这一情况在持续监测中仍未得到解决。

news.title: 異常斷魂!屏東確診H5N1「撲殺4.9萬隻鵪鶉」業者心死
news.excerpt: 屏東縣鹽埔鄉一處鵪鶉場主動通報異常死亡,經採檢確診感染H5N1亞型高病原禽流感病毒。屏東縣動物防疫所已於2日緊急出動,現場撲殺高達4萬8977隻鵪鶉,並全面啟動移動管制與場區周邊消毒作業。農業處提醒,每年10月至3月為禽流感好發期,呼籲業者務必落實生物安全防疫措施,加強自主健康觀察,若發現異狀應盡速通報,共同防範疫情擴散。

另一方面進行移動管制、對場區及周邊進行噴灑消毒作業,採集檢體送農業部獸醫研究所檢驗,並同步啟動該場半徑1公里內周圍養禽場監測採樣工作及周邊半徑3公里進行訪視輔導,訪查轄內禽場有無可疑病例,以確認周圍場家禽健康情形及有無病毒活動,並持續加強高風險養禽鄉鎮養禽場周邊環境消毒,以控制疫情散播。 analysis.brief_en: A poultry farm in Pingtung County, Yilan, reported an outbreak of H5N1 avian influenza, leading to the culling of 48,977 quails. The incident was confirmed by the Pingtung County Animal Quarantine Station, which initiated a series of measures including movement restrictions, environmental disinfection, and monitoring of surrounding poultry farms. The culling has resulted in significant financial losses for the operator, who expressed deep sorrow. The response includes ongoing surveillance and control efforts to prevent further spread of the virus. The event occurred on November 2, 2026, and was reported on November 3, 2026. The outbreak highlights the need for strict biosecurity measures in poultry farming, as H5N1 is a highly pathogenic avian influenza virus known for its severe impact on bird populations and potential zoonotic risks.

news.content_zh: 宜兰屏东县一养鸡场报告禽流感H5N1 暴发,导致48,977只鹌鹑被扑杀。屏东县动物检疫站证实此事,并启动限制行动、环境消毒、周边家禽养殖场监控等一系列措施。此次扑杀给运营商造成了重大经济损失,运营商表示深感悲痛。应对措施包括持续进行的 监测 和控制措施,以防止病毒进一步传播。该事件发生于 2026 年 11 月 2 日,并于 2026 年 11 月 3 日进行报道。暴发 强调在家禽养殖中采取严格的生物安全措施的必要性,因为 H5N1 是一种 高致病性禽流感 病毒,以其对鸟类种群的严重影响和潜在的人畜共患风险而闻名。

死者是華盛頓州亞基馬縣居民,生前有基礎疾病,在一家有感染禽流感牛隻的奶牛場接觸到病毒。美國疾病控制和預防中心周一(2日)確認,分析死者體內的病毒基因序列後未發現任何可能導致病毒更容易傳播或引發更嚴重疾病變異。亞基馬縣近期出現3宗人類感染禽流感病例,均與一家奶牛場有關,衞生官員正追蹤感染者的密切接觸人士,並監測他們的症狀。

H5型禽流感在全球野生鳥類中廣泛傳播,並已在家禽和奶牛中引發疫情。前年初迄今美國已報告超過70宗人類感染禽流感病毒病例,其中兩人於去年1月和11月死亡,他們分別感染H5N1型和H5N5型禽流感病毒。

死者是華盛頓州亞基馬縣居民,生前有基礎疾病,在一家有感染禽流感牛隻的奶牛場接觸到病毒。美國疾病控制和預防中心周一(2日)確認,分析死者體內的病毒基因序列後未發現任何可能導致病毒更容易傳播或引發更嚴重疾病變異。亞基馬縣近期出現3宗人類感染禽流感病例,均與一家奶牛場有關,衞生官員正追蹤感染者的密切接觸人士,並監測他們的症狀。

Google 偏好來源 (另開新視窗) 將 Yahoo 加入 Google 優先推薦來源 將 Yahoo 設為首選來源,在 Google 上查看更多我們的精彩報導 加入首選來源(另開新視窗) 屏東縣鹽埔鄉一處鵪鶉場11月1日確診感染H5N1亞型高病原禽流感病毒,屏東縣動物防疫所隨即於11月2日執行撲殺4萬8977隻鵪鶉,並完成清潔消毒與追蹤。 屏東縣鹽埔鄉一處鵪鶉場11月1日確診感染H5N1亞型高病原禽流感病毒,屏東縣動物防疫所隨即於11月2日執行撲殺4萬8977隻鵪鶉。(圖/屏東縣動物防疫所提供) 該鵪鶉場於10月30日主動通報出現異常死亡情形,動物防疫所依標準作業程序前往採集檢體送驗,實施移動管制與場區消毒。經農業部獸醫研究所檢驗確認感染H5N1,防疫單位隔日展開處置。 本次現場共撲殺4萬8977隻鵪鶉,內容包含種禽6500隻、產蛋鵪鶉2萬77隻及未產蛋鵪鶉2萬2400隻,防疫規模相當龐大。 廣告 廣告 為防止疫情蔓延,動物防疫所針對案場半徑1公里內的養禽場進行監測採樣,確認禽隻健康狀況;半徑3公里內的養禽場則進行訪視輔導與可疑病例訪查,同時加強高風險鄉鎮養禽場周邊環境消毒。 屏東縣政府農業處長李永文表示,每年10月至隔年3月為禽流感好發季節,養禽業者須落實生物安全措施,嚴格消毒進出人員與車輛,並維持防鳥圍網正常運作以避免野鳥接觸。 李永文強調,業者每日應自主觀察家禽健康,若發現精神沉鬱、食慾不振、產蛋率下降或異常死亡,應立即通報動物防疫所,切勿隱匿,才能及早處置控制疫情。 原文出處:屏東鵪鶉場爆H5N1禽流感!縣府緊急撲殺4.8萬隻 完成清消 更多中天新聞網報導 屏東縣鹽埔鄉一處鵪鶉場11月1日確診感染H5N1亞型高病原禽流感病毒,屏東縣動物防疫所隨即於11月2日執行撲殺4萬8977隻鵪鶉。(圖/屏東縣動物防疫所提供) 該鵪鶉場於10月30日主動通報出現異常死亡情形,動物防疫所依標準作業程序前往採集檢體送驗,實施移動管制與場區消毒。經農業部獸醫研究所檢驗確認感染H5N1,防疫單位隔日展開處置。 news.source_body_en: A pigeon farm in Yantou County, Taiwan, confirmed an H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza virus infection on November 1, 2026. The county government immediately culled 48,977 pigeons and implemented monitoring and disinfection measures within a 3-kilometer radius of the affected farm. Authorities emphasized the need for poultry farmers to enhance biosecurity measures to prevent further spread.

屏東縣動物防疫所10月30日接獲鹽埔鄉1處鵪鶉場主動通報飼養鵪鶉異常死亡,隨即依標準作業程序啟動防疫機制,11月1日經研究所確認感染H5N1亞型高病原禽流感病毒,2日撲殺作業,共撲殺4萬8977隻鵪鶉,並督導業者完成場區清潔與消毒。 屏東縣動防所表示,接獲禽場通報,派人到該場移動管制、對場區及周邊噴灑消毒,採集檢體送農業部獸醫研究所檢驗,同步啟動該場半徑1公里內周圍養禽場監測採樣工作及周邊半徑3公里進行訪視輔導,訪查轄內禽場有無可疑病例,以確認周圍場家禽健康情形及有無病毒活動,並持續加強高風險養禽鄉鎮養禽場周邊環境消毒,以控制疫情散播。 動防所表示,2日撲殺,共撲殺4萬8977隻鵪鶉(種禽6500隻、產蛋鵪鶉2萬77隻、未產蛋鵪鶉2萬2400隻),並再次督導業者完成場區清潔及消毒工作,及對相關聯場進行回溯追蹤以降低疫情傳播風險。 農業處長李永文表示,每年10月至3月為禽流感好發季節,提醒養禽業者須落實各項生物安全措施做好人員管制,消毒人員、車輛、運輸工具及其他進出禽場器具,維持防鳥圍網設施運作,每日自主觀察場內家禽健康狀況,若發現異常症狀(如精神沉鬱、食慾不振、產蛋率下降或異常死亡等),請盡速通報動物防疫所,以利控制及防範疫情蔓延。 屏東縣 禽流感 登入後開始簽到 會員來簽到 您即將前往會員中心 登入簽到送 LINE She built Vet Candy as a community-first media brand and it has grown to become the leading platform for the next generation of veterinary professionals. How do I join Vet Candy? supplementary_news.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, November 05, 2026 EID Journal: Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 #19,402 In the spring of 2024 a mysterious illness spreading among Texas, Kansas, and New Mexico dairy cattle was identified as avian H5N1, an outbreak that has now spread to at least 21 states, and has affected > 1200 herds. At that time cattle were believed poorly susceptible to influenza A (see A Brief History Of Influenza A In Cattle/Ruminants), and so testing for H5N1 was delayed. The immediate global reaction was that this was an `American problem', caused by a new (and presumably unique to North America) strain (B3.13) of H5N1 (see DEFRA Risk Assessment Of HPAI H5N1 Occurring in Cattle In the UK), and unlikely to occur in Europe. This strain has not been detected in the UK, and none of the viruses detected in the UK over the 2020 to 2024 HPAI outbreak period have contained genetic material originating from North or South American viruses. The risk to GB of H5N1 in livestock is assessed at very low. That assumption was challenged in June of 2024 (see Germany: FLI Statement On Experimental Infection Of Dairy Cows With European H5N1 Virus) when researchers demonstrated that a German virus isolate could replicate in a cow's udder after experimental infection. Over the summer of 2024 the USDA reassuringly suggested that B3.13 entered dairy cattle via a single spillover from birds - and was subsequently spread by the interstate transport of infected dairy cows. That assumption held until early 2025 when another genotype (D1.1) turned up in dairy cattle in two states (Nevada & Arizona). In March of 2025, the UK's Defra reported H5N1 Detected In Domestic Sheep with Mastitis, and over the previous year we'd seen reports of other non-B3.13 H5N1 in goats and sheep in Pakistan, horses in Mongolia, and pigs in Oregon. Also in the spring of 2025, Chinese scientists warned that Clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI H5N1 influenza Viruses from Birds in China Replicated Effectively in Bovine cells. Last April, in Preprint: Infection of the Bovine Mammary Gland by Avian H5N1 Subclade 2.3.4.4b Influenza viruses. we saw even more evidence that diverse HPAI H5 strains could infect dairy cattle. The authors wrote: Our findings show that mammary tissue from common cattle breeds is permissive to clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 infection. These results support the view that bovine mammary epithelium represents a susceptible tissue environment and suggest that IAV infection in cattle may be more widespread than previously assumed. Four months ago, in Eurosurveillance: Detection of antibodies against avian influenza in European dairy cattle, the Netherlands, January 2026), we saw additional evidence of HPAI spillover into dairy cattle outside of the United States. A little over a a year ago, WOAH embraced an 11-page OFFLU technical document (see OFFLU Guidelines for High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Virus Risk Mitigation in Cattle) which - among other things - finally made HPAI in cattle a `reportable disease'. But surveillance remains passive, and testing largely up to the discretion of the livestock owner. Something that many farmers find unappealing, fearing the quarantining of their herds and the stigma of infection. Today we've an EID Journal research letter which reports compelling serological evidence not only of HPAI H5 infection in Egyptian cattle, but LPAI H9N2 as well. The authors write: Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Testing included both hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays, and positive results weren't confined to cattle. Sheep and goats tested positive for LPAI H9N2 as well. I've only posted some excerpts from this letter. Follow the link to read it in its entirety. I'll have a postscript after the break. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 Mokhtar Gomaa, Rabeh El-Shesheny, Ahmed El Taweel, Omnia Kutkat, Hager Emam, Basant Helal, Ayat Swelam, Mohamed GabAllah, Ahmed Kandeil, Pamela P. McKenzie, Richard J. Webby, Mohamed Ahmed Ali, and Ghazi Kayali Abstract Spillover of influenza A(H5N1) virus to cattle in the United States sparked global concern. We investigated whether endemic avian influenza viruses are potentially spilling over into domestic livestock in Egypt. We detected influenza H9N2 antibodies in 2.5% and H5N1 antibodies in 2.9%–4.5% of tested animals. Additional surveillance will elucidate host infection dynamics. (SNIP) Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus and low-pathogenicity avian influenza A(H9N2) virus are widely and endemically circulating in poultry in Egypt on farms and backyards and at live bird markets (7). Subtype H5N1 was detected in feral rats in poultry production areas (8). In addition, reassortment events between the H5N1 and H9N2 subtypes led to the emergence of novel clade 2.3.4.4b influenza A(H5N2) viruses (9). To determine whether those viruses are spilling over to livestock in Egypt, particularly in mixed-species settings, we conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt. During October 2024–January 2026, we collected 444 serum samples from 33 conveniently selected small farms (≈10 cattle, no mixed species) and backyards housing cattle (1–3 cattle with mixed species) in 3 governorates (n = 155, n = 59, and n = 230) in northern Egypt, representing common practices in Egypt. Sheep and goats were also sampled if housed in the same backyards as cattle. All sampled animals were apparently healthy adults. We tested serum samples for antibodies against a 2025 Egyptian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 (A/duck/Egypt/BA20361C/2022) virus using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays and against a G1-like Egypt influenza A(H9N2) (A/chicken/Egypt/RA20191OP/2022) virus by HI in accordance with World Health Organization protocols (10). We considered an antibody titer >1:40 as positive for both assays. Data on the number of cows, presence of other mammals (e.g., donkeys and horses), and presence of avian species (poultry and/or wild birds) were available for 271 samples. We performed statistical comparisons with χ2 or Fisher exact tests; we considered p<0.05 statistically significant. Overall, 11 (2.5%) serum specimens tested positive for influenza A(H9N2) antibodies, 20 (4.5%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by HI, and 13 (2.9%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by MN (Figure, panel A). Positive titers were 40–160 (Figure, panel B). None of the samples tested positive for antibodies against both viruses. Of the 20 H5N1 virus specimens positive by HI, 12 tested positive by MN; 1 specimen was negative by HI and positive by MN. All influenza H9N2-positive specimens were from 3 locations in the same governorate (p = 0.005). Influenza A(H5N1) antibodies were detected in 2 governorates; the differences in detection rates by governorate were statistically significant (0%, 1.3%, and 4.8%; p = 0.049). All H5N1 virus–seropositive specimens were from cattle (Table). We detected H9N2 antibodies in 6/374 (1.6%) of cattle specimens, 1/31 (3.2%) of goat specimens, and 4/39 (10.3%) of sheep specimens (p = 0.004). Presence of other animals did not predict seropositivity. Small farms had a significantly higher proportion of H5N1 virus–positive animals tested by MN (p = 0.039). Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus of the EA-2021-AB genotype and G1-like H9N2 virus appear to be spilling over into livestock in Egypt; however, because our evidence is serologic, we could not ascertain whether true infection is occurring and whether the same signs seen in the United States are common in cattle in Egypt. Even so, the evidence is a strong indicator that spillover is occurring, similar to that reported in Europe (4,6). Furthermore, spillover is not restricted to cattle; some sheep and goats tested in our study were seropositive for influenza A(H9N2) virus. Surveillance for avian influenza viruses in Egypt and other countries, especially those in which avian influenza is endemic, will verify infection and provide data on frequency, routes of transmission, and factors affecting infection of and transmission to livestock. (Continue . . . ) Despite the accrued evidence to date - for a myriad of political, societal, economic, and logistical reasons - governments around the world appear slow to respond to HPAI (and now LPAI) spillover into mammalian livestock. We see this same reluctance in investigating HPAI spillover into other species, including farmed mink (see Virological (Referral): Preliminary report on H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in Utah mink, August 2026). Although this laissez faire approach may work out in the short run, it provides these viruses with ample opportunities to spread, to evolve, and to adapt. Admittedly, most of these viruses will likely never pose a serious public health threat. But it only takes one overachiever - aided and abetted by inaction on our part - to plunge the world back into another pandemic crisis. Wednesday, November 04, 2026 NOAA Climate Prediction: West Coast Atmospheric River Event (Nov 10th-16th) NOAA Forecast Issued Nov 3rd #19,401 As we discussed 2 months ago in #NPM26: Preparing For An El Niño Winter, the west coast and the southern tier of states have been warned to expect an unusually wet and stormy winter due to the record Pacific El Niño. Predicting exactly where unusual or severe weather will occur this winter is impossible, but generally, the jet stream across the United States shifts storm tracks to the southern tier of states during an El Niño winter. Parts of Florida have already seen record flooding in the past week, but it appears that next week Northern California and the Pacific Northwest will be faced with a substantial atmospheric river event; one which could bring heavy rain and snow to much of the west coast. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center published the following warning yesterday: Key Messages from the NOAA Climate Prediction Center Issued November 2, 2026 and Updated November 3, 2026 Atmospheric River Expected to Affect the West Coast States Atmospheric river activity is expected to pull significant amounts of moisture into much of the West Coast during the second week of November and weekend, with a potential secondary moisture surge later in the period. Strong surface low pressure just north of the region will also likely drive high winds along the immediate coastline. (a) A moderate risk (40 to 60%) of heavy precipitation and possible flooding is indicated for Nov 11 to 15 across parts of the Pacific Northwest and northern/central California, while a slight risk (20 to 40%) extends to Nov 17 across the West Coast into the Desert Southwest, Great Basin, and Southern Rockies. High winds are possible across much of the West, including a moderate risk along the immediate West Coast Nov 11 to 15 and a broader slight risk extending to Nov 17. (b) A moderate risk of heavy snow is indicated across the higher elevations of the Klamath and Sierra Nevada Nov 11 to 15. Slight risks of heavy snow extend to Nov 17 for high elevations of the Cascades, Klamath, and Sierra Nevada, as well as the Northern Intermountain, Great Basin, and Central and Northern Rockies. Monitor local forecasts for safety alerts, avoid driving through flooded roadways, and use caution if traveling through high elevations. Be prepared for power outages due to high winds. This is likely just the first of many such storms expected to impact the west coast this winter, and inland freshwater flooding is a major concern. Six weeks ago, in anticipation of these events, California Declared a State of Emergency to Bolster Statewide El Niño Preparedness. The LA County website is urging both community and individual preparedness for what is expected to be a difficult winter, and advises: LA County is preparing its flood control and emergency response systems now. Crews are inspecting and maintaining dams, debris basins, channels, storm drains, and pump stations; monitoring burn areas, hillsides, and other areas at risk of flooding and debris flows; and preparing for evacuations, emergency shelter, and other storm response. County teams are also preparing to assist people experiencing homelessness, older adults, and others who may need additional help during severe weather. Here’s what residents can do now: Sign up for emergency alerts: Go to alert.lacounty.gov to receive emergency notifications, including evacuation warnings and orders. Know the risks where you live: If you are near a hillside, canyon, recent burn area, or area that can flood, learn your flood and mudflow risk before a storm. Make an evacuation plan: Know where you will go and how you will get there if you need to leave quickly. Have supplies ready: Keep enough food, water, medications, and other essentials for up to 10 days. Prepare your home: Clear gutters, downspouts, and storm drains, fix roof leaks, and get sandbags before heavy rain is in the forecast. Consider flood insurance: Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Flood insurance is separate and can take at least 30 days to go into effect. Need help with mud or debris flow risk? Call LA County Public Works at 1-800-933-0930 to speak with an engineer. Know someone experiencing homelessness who needs help? Visit homeless.lacounty.gov/get-help/ While this first round is expected to impact further north, now is the time for everyone along the west coast - and much of the southern United States - to prepare for severe storms and elevated flood risks. Those interested in diving into one of the more extreme (albeit, based on historic events) scenarios of Atmospheric river flooding may wish to revisit 2022's California's ARkStorm Scenario Revisited & National Preparedness Month, but even a far less severe event could be devastating. Whether it's coastal storms, inland flooding, or ice storms or tornado outbreaks in the southland, El Niño has the potential to adversely affect millions of Americans this winter (and potentially billions worldwide). So, if the power goes out today for a week, or if flood waters begin to rise . . . do you already have? A battery operated NWS Emergency Radio to find out what was going on, and to get vital instructions from emergency officials A decent first-aid kit, so that you can treat injuries Enough non-perishable food and water on hand to feed and hydrate your family (including pets) for the duration A way to provide light when the grid is down. A way to cook safely without electricity A way to purify or filter water A way to handle basic sanitation and waste disposal. A way to stay cool (fans) or warm when the power is out. A small supply of cash to use in case credit/debit machines are not working An emergency plan, including meeting places, emergency out-of-state contact numbers, a disaster buddy, and in case you must evacuate, a bug-out bag Spare supply of essential prescription medicines that you or your family may need A way to entertain yourself, or your kids, during a prolonged blackout If not, you've got some important work to do. A good place to get started is by visiting Ready.gov, or by hitting this link which will serve up a series of my preparedness blogs. When Flu Viruses Collide Antigenic `Shift' or Reassortment #19,400 Influenza co-infections in humans - or in any other susceptible host (birds, pigs, cattle, sheep, etc.) - are a public health concern because they can allow two (or more) influenza viruses to swap genetic material (reassort) and produce a hybrid virus. It's more than just a theoretical concern, as twice in my lifetime (1957 & 1968) a reassortment between seasonal flu and an avian flu virus - possibly in a human host - produced a pandemic virus. The first (1957) was pandemic H2N2, which According to the CDC emerged after three different genes from an H2N2 avian influenza A virus combined with 5 genes from the existing H1N1 virus. In 1968 a novel H3N2 virus emerged (a reassortment consisting of 2 genes from a low path avian influenza H3 virus, and 6 genes from seasonal H2N2) which continues to spark yearly epidemics more than 58 years later. While we'll never know exactly where or how these novel viruses came about, the genetic fingerprints of reassortment are unmistakable. This is the reason why yearly flu vaccination has long been recommended for people who raise pigs or work with poultry and the CDC now urges vaccination in dairy workers. Coinfection is rare, but not unheard of, and as any virologist will tell you; Shift happens. With three recent dairy-linked H5N1 cases (1 fatal) reported in Washington state - and previous evidence suggesting mild and/or asymptomatic cases may go unreported (see MMWR: Serologic Evidence of Recent Infection with HPAI A(H5) Virus Among Dairy Workers), the arrival of the fall flu season raises concerns over the possibility of seeing a rare coinfection. In addition to vaccination, the CDC also promotes (see Reducing Exposure for Workers to Avian Influenza A Viruses) the use of PPEs, but it isn't clear how many are following this advice. Since 2009, with increased surveillance and better tools, we've seen a growing number of reports of human co-infection with influenza A: EID Journal: Nosocomial Co-Transmission Of H7N9 & H1N1pdm09 EID Journal: Human Co-Infection with Avian and Seasonal Influenza Viruses, China Lancet: Coinfection With H7N9 & H3N2…

Is Vet Candy really free? Yes. Membership is completely free. No credit card, no trial period, no catch. supplementary_news.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, November 05, 2026 EID Journal: Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 #19,402 In the spring of 2024 a mysterious illness spreading among Texas, Kansas, and New Mexico dairy cattle was identified as avian H5N1, an outbreak that has now spread to at least 21 states, and has affected > 1200 herds. At that time cattle were believed poorly susceptible to influenza A (see A Brief History Of Influenza A In Cattle/Ruminants), and so testing for H5N1 was delayed. The immediate global reaction was that this was an `American problem', caused by a new (and presumably unique to North America) strain (B3.13) of H5N1 (see DEFRA Risk Assessment Of HPAI H5N1 Occurring in Cattle In the UK), and unlikely to occur in Europe. This strain has not been detected in the UK, and none of the viruses detected in the UK over the 2020 to 2024 HPAI outbreak period have contained genetic material originating from North or South American viruses. The risk to GB of H5N1 in livestock is assessed at very low. That assumption was challenged in June of 2024 (see Germany: FLI Statement On Experimental Infection Of Dairy Cows With European H5N1 Virus) when researchers demonstrated that a German virus isolate could replicate in a cow's udder after experimental infection. Over the summer of 2024 the USDA reassuringly suggested that B3.13 entered dairy cattle via a single spillover from birds - and was subsequently spread by the interstate transport of infected dairy cows. That assumption held until early 2025 when another genotype (D1.1) turned up in dairy cattle in two states (Nevada & Arizona). In March of 2025, the UK's Defra reported H5N1 Detected In Domestic Sheep with Mastitis, and over the previous year we'd seen reports of other non-B3.13 H5N1 in goats and sheep in Pakistan, horses in Mongolia, and pigs in Oregon. Also in the spring of 2025, Chinese scientists warned that Clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI H5N1 influenza Viruses from Birds in China Replicated Effectively in Bovine cells. Last April, in Preprint: Infection of the Bovine Mammary Gland by Avian H5N1 Subclade 2.3.4.4b Influenza viruses. we saw even more evidence that diverse HPAI H5 strains could infect dairy cattle. The authors wrote: Our findings show that mammary tissue from common cattle breeds is permissive to clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 infection. These results support the view that bovine mammary epithelium represents a susceptible tissue environment and suggest that IAV infection in cattle may be more widespread than previously assumed. Four months ago, in Eurosurveillance: Detection of antibodies against avian influenza in European dairy cattle, the Netherlands, January 2026), we saw additional evidence of HPAI spillover into dairy cattle outside of the United States. A little over a a year ago, WOAH embraced an 11-page OFFLU technical document (see OFFLU Guidelines for High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Virus Risk Mitigation in Cattle) which - among other things - finally made HPAI in cattle a `reportable disease'. But surveillance remains passive, and testing largely up to the discretion of the livestock owner. Something that many farmers find unappealing, fearing the quarantining of their herds and the stigma of infection. Today we've an EID Journal research letter which reports compelling serological evidence not only of HPAI H5 infection in Egyptian cattle, but LPAI H9N2 as well. The authors write: Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Testing included both hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays, and positive results weren't confined to cattle. Sheep and goats tested positive for LPAI H9N2 as well. I've only posted some excerpts from this letter. Follow the link to read it in its entirety. I'll have a postscript after the break. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 Mokhtar Gomaa, Rabeh El-Shesheny, Ahmed El Taweel, Omnia Kutkat, Hager Emam, Basant Helal, Ayat Swelam, Mohamed GabAllah, Ahmed Kandeil, Pamela P. McKenzie, Richard J. Webby, Mohamed Ahmed Ali, and Ghazi Kayali Abstract Spillover of influenza A(H5N1) virus to cattle in the United States sparked global concern. We investigated whether endemic avian influenza viruses are potentially spilling over into domestic livestock in Egypt. We detected influenza H9N2 antibodies in 2.5% and H5N1 antibodies in 2.9%–4.5% of tested animals. Additional surveillance will elucidate host infection dynamics. (SNIP) Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus and low-pathogenicity avian influenza A(H9N2) virus are widely and endemically circulating in poultry in Egypt on farms and backyards and at live bird markets (7). Subtype H5N1 was detected in feral rats in poultry production areas (8). In addition, reassortment events between the H5N1 and H9N2 subtypes led to the emergence of novel clade 2.3.4.4b influenza A(H5N2) viruses (9). To determine whether those viruses are spilling over to livestock in Egypt, particularly in mixed-species settings, we conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt. During October 2024–January 2026, we collected 444 serum samples from 33 conveniently selected small farms (≈10 cattle, no mixed species) and backyards housing cattle (1–3 cattle with mixed species) in 3 governorates (n = 155, n = 59, and n = 230) in northern Egypt, representing common practices in Egypt. Sheep and goats were also sampled if housed in the same backyards as cattle. All sampled animals were apparently healthy adults. We tested serum samples for antibodies against a 2025 Egyptian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 (A/duck/Egypt/BA20361C/2022) virus using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays and against a G1-like Egypt influenza A(H9N2) (A/chicken/Egypt/RA20191OP/2022) virus by HI in accordance with World Health Organization protocols (10). We considered an antibody titer >1:40 as positive for both assays. Data on the number of cows, presence of other mammals (e.g., donkeys and horses), and presence of avian species (poultry and/or wild birds) were available for 271 samples. We performed statistical comparisons with χ2 or Fisher exact tests; we considered p<0.05 statistically significant. Overall, 11 (2.5%) serum specimens tested positive for influenza A(H9N2) antibodies, 20 (4.5%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by HI, and 13 (2.9%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by MN (Figure, panel A). Positive titers were 40–160 (Figure, panel B). None of the samples tested positive for antibodies against both viruses. Of the 20 H5N1 virus specimens positive by HI, 12 tested positive by MN; 1 specimen was negative by HI and positive by MN. All influenza H9N2-positive specimens were from 3 locations in the same governorate (p = 0.005). Influenza A(H5N1) antibodies were detected in 2 governorates; the differences in detection rates by governorate were statistically significant (0%, 1.3%, and 4.8%; p = 0.049). All H5N1 virus–seropositive specimens were from cattle (Table). We detected H9N2 antibodies in 6/374 (1.6%) of cattle specimens, 1/31 (3.2%) of goat specimens, and 4/39 (10.3%) of sheep specimens (p = 0.004). Presence of other animals did not predict seropositivity. Small farms had a significantly higher proportion of H5N1 virus–positive animals tested by MN (p = 0.039). Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus of the EA-2021-AB genotype and G1-like H9N2 virus appear to be spilling over into livestock in Egypt; however, because our evidence is serologic, we could not ascertain whether true infection is occurring and whether the same signs seen in the United States are common in cattle in Egypt. Even so, the evidence is a strong indicator that spillover is occurring, similar to that reported in Europe (4,6). Furthermore, spillover is not restricted to cattle; some sheep and goats tested in our study were seropositive for influenza A(H9N2) virus. Surveillance for avian influenza viruses in Egypt and other countries, especially those in which avian influenza is endemic, will verify infection and provide data on frequency, routes of transmission, and factors affecting infection of and transmission to livestock. (Continue . . . ) Despite the accrued evidence to date - for a myriad of political, societal, economic, and logistical reasons - governments around the world appear slow to respond to HPAI (and now LPAI) spillover into mammalian livestock. We see this same reluctance in investigating HPAI spillover into other species, including farmed mink (see Virological (Referral): Preliminary report on H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in Utah mink, August 2026). Although this laissez faire approach may work out in the short run, it provides these viruses with ample opportunities to spread, to evolve, and to adapt. Admittedly, most of these viruses will likely never pose a serious public health threat. But it only takes one overachiever - aided and abetted by inaction on our part - to plunge the world back into another pandemic crisis. Wednesday, November 04, 2026 NOAA Climate Prediction: West Coast Atmospheric River Event (Nov 10th-16th) NOAA Forecast Issued Nov 3rd #19,401 As we discussed 2 months ago in #NPM26: Preparing For An El Niño Winter, the west coast and the southern tier of states have been warned to expect an unusually wet and stormy winter due to the record Pacific El Niño. Predicting exactly where unusual or severe weather will occur this winter is impossible, but generally, the jet stream across the United States shifts storm tracks to the southern tier of states during an El Niño winter. Parts of Florida have already seen record flooding in the past week, but it appears that next week Northern California and the Pacific Northwest will be faced with a substantial atmospheric river event; one which could bring heavy rain and snow to much of the west coast. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center published the following warning yesterday: Key Messages from the NOAA Climate Prediction Center Issued November 2, 2026 and Updated November 3, 2026 Atmospheric River Expected to Affect the West Coast States Atmospheric river activity is expected to pull significant amounts of moisture into much of the West Coast during the second week of November and weekend, with a potential secondary moisture surge later in the period. Strong surface low pressure just north of the region will also likely drive high winds along the immediate coastline. (a) A moderate risk (40 to 60%) of heavy precipitation and possible flooding is indicated for Nov 11 to 15 across parts of the Pacific Northwest and northern/central California, while a slight risk (20 to 40%) extends to Nov 17 across the West Coast into the Desert Southwest, Great Basin, and Southern Rockies. High winds are possible across much of the West, including a moderate risk along the immediate West Coast Nov 11 to 15 and a broader slight risk extending to Nov 17. (b) A moderate risk of heavy snow is indicated across the higher elevations of the Klamath and Sierra Nevada Nov 11 to 15. Slight risks of heavy snow extend to Nov 17 for high elevations of the Cascades, Klamath, and Sierra Nevada, as well as the Northern Intermountain, Great Basin, and Central and Northern Rockies. Monitor local forecasts for safety alerts, avoid driving through flooded roadways, and use caution if traveling through high elevations. Be prepared for power outages due to high winds. This is likely just the first of many such storms expected to impact the west coast this winter, and inland freshwater flooding is a major concern. Six weeks ago, in anticipation of these events, California Declared a State of Emergency to Bolster Statewide El Niño Preparedness. The LA County website is urging both community and individual preparedness for what is expected to be a difficult winter, and advises: LA County is preparing its flood control and emergency response systems now. Crews are inspecting and maintaining dams, debris basins, channels, storm drains, and pump stations; monitoring burn areas, hillsides, and other areas at risk of flooding and debris flows; and preparing for evacuations, emergency shelter, and other storm response. County teams are also preparing to assist people experiencing homelessness, older adults, and others who may need additional help during severe weather. Here’s what residents can do now: Sign up for emergency alerts: Go to alert.lacounty.gov to receive emergency notifications, including evacuation warnings and orders. Know the risks where you live: If you are near a hillside, canyon, recent burn area, or area that can flood, learn your flood and mudflow risk before a storm. Make an evacuation plan: Know where you will go and how you will get there if you need to leave quickly. Have supplies ready: Keep enough food, water, medications, and other essentials for up to 10 days. Prepare your home: Clear gutters, downspouts, and storm drains, fix roof leaks, and get sandbags before heavy rain is in the forecast. Consider flood insurance: Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Flood insurance is separate and can take at least 30 days to go into effect. Need help with mud or debris flow risk? Call LA County Public Works at 1-800-933-0930 to speak with an engineer. Know someone experiencing homelessness who needs help? Visit homeless.lacounty.gov/get-help/ While this first round is expected to impact further north, now is the time for everyone along the west coast - and much of the southern United States - to prepare for severe storms and elevated flood risks. Those interested in diving into one of the more extreme (albeit, based on historic events) scenarios of Atmospheric river flooding may wish to revisit 2022's California's ARkStorm Scenario Revisited & National Preparedness Month, but even a far less severe event could be devastating. Whether it's coastal storms, inland flooding, or ice storms or tornado outbreaks in the southland, El Niño has the potential to adversely affect millions of Americans this winter (and potentially billions worldwide). So, if the power goes out today for a week, or if flood waters begin to rise . . . do you already have? A battery operated NWS Emergency Radio to find out what was going on, and to get vital instructions from emergency officials A decent first-aid kit, so that you can treat injuries Enough non-perishable food and water on hand to feed and hydrate your family (including pets) for the duration A way to provide light when the grid is down. A way to cook safely without electricity A way to purify or filter water A way to handle basic sanitation and waste disposal. A way to stay cool (fans) or warm when the power is out. A small supply of cash to use in case credit/debit machines are not working An emergency plan, including meeting places, emergency out-of-state contact numbers, a disaster buddy, and in case you must evacuate, a bug-out bag Spare supply of essential prescription medicines that you or your family may need A way to entertain yourself, or your kids, during a prolonged blackout If not, you've got some important work to do. A good place to get started is by visiting Ready.gov, or by hitting this link which will serve up a series of my preparedness blogs. When Flu Viruses Collide Antigenic `Shift' or Reassortment #19,400 Influenza co-infections in humans - or in any other susceptible host (birds, pigs, cattle, sheep, etc.) - are a public health concern because they can allow two (or more) influenza viruses to swap genetic material (reassort) and produce a hybrid virus. It's more than just a theoretical concern, as twice in my lifetime (1957 & 1968) a reassortment between seasonal flu and an avian flu virus - possibly in a human host - produced a pandemic virus. The first (1957) was pandemic H2N2, which According to the CDC emerged after three different genes from an H2N2 avian influenza A virus combined with 5 genes from the existing H1N1 virus. In 1968 a novel H3N2 virus emerged (a reassortment consisting of 2 genes from a low path avian influenza H3 virus, and 6 genes from seasonal H2N2) which continues to spark yearly epidemics more than 58 years later. While we'll never know exactly where or how these novel viruses came about, the genetic fingerprints of reassortment are unmistakable. This is the reason why yearly flu vaccination has long been recommended for people who raise pigs or work with poultry and the CDC now urges vaccination in dairy workers. Coinfection is rare, but not unheard of, and as any virologist will tell you; Shift happens. With three recent dairy-linked H5N1 cases (1 fatal) reported in Washington state - and previous evidence suggesting mild and/or asymptomatic cases may go unreported (see MMWR: Serologic Evidence of Recent Infection with HPAI A(H5) Virus Among Dairy Workers), the arrival of the fall flu season raises concerns over the possibility of seeing a rare coinfection. In addition to vaccination, the CDC also promotes (see Reducing Exposure for Workers to Avian Influenza A Viruses) the use of PPEs, but it isn't clear how many are following this advice. Since 2009, with increased surveillance and better tools, we've seen a growing number of reports of human co-infection with influenza A: EID Journal: Nosocomial Co-Transmission Of H7N9 & H1N1pdm09 EID Journal: Human Co-Infection with Avian and Seasonal Influenza Viruses, China Lancet: Coinfection With H7N9 & H3N2…
